steps.detail: The data need not be an array: any range with a yes-or-no test that flips once can be halved. Here the test is mid squared being at most 2000, and the answer is 44 because 44 squared is 1936 and 45 squared is 2025. This pattern answers a surprising share of hard problems.
steps.proof: You get 44, with 1936 under 2000 and 2025 over it.
steps.pitfall: Using this where the test does not flip monotonically, which makes halving unsound.

problems.prompt: What is the integer square root of 2000?
What property must the yes-or-no test have across 1 to 2000?
problems.answer: It must flip once across the range and stay flipped.

problems.prompt: Roughly how many steps does searching 1 to 2000 take?
problems.answer: About 11, since log2(2000) is close to 11.

steps.title: Search a Rotated Array
steps.mastery: Binary search data that is sorted but rotated.
steps.practice: Find 1 in [4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2] by deciding at each step which half is in order.
steps.detail: Compare the middle with the ends to see which half is sorted, then check whether the target lies inside that half: if it does, search there, otherwise search the other. The rotation point is what the ordinary search assumes does not exist.
steps.proof: You find 1 at index 4.
steps.pitfall: Running a plain binary search, which walks into the unsorted half and misses the target.

problems.prompt: A rotated array [4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2] is searched for 1. Which index holds it?
problems.answer: Index 4.

problems.prompt: With mid at index 2 of that array, which half is in ascending order?
problems.answer: The left half, 4 to 6.

problems.prompt: Which assumption of a plain binary search does a rotation at index 4 break?
problems.answer: That the whole range is in ascending order.

steps.title: Count the Steps
steps.mastery: State how many comparisons a binary search needs.
steps.practice: Work out the maximum comparisons for 1000, 1,000,000 and 1,000,000,000 sorted items.
steps.detail: It is log2 of n rounded up: about 10, 20 and 30. Those 3 numbers are worth memorising, because they are the reason an index on a billion rows is fast and the reason a linear scan of the same data is not.
steps.proof: About 10, 20 and 30 comparisons.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a thousandfold more data means a thousandfold more work, when it means 10 more comparisons.

problems.prompt: At most how many comparisons to binary search 1,000,000 sorted items?
problems.answer: About 20.

problems.prompt: Going from 1000 items to 1,000,000 adds how many comparisons?
problems.answer: About 10.

problems.prompt: 1,000,000,000 sorted rows need at most how many halvings?
problems.answer: About 30.

steps.title: Check the Precondition
steps.mastery: Establish that data is sorted before searching it.
steps.practice: Run a binary search on the unsorted [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] for 4 and explain the result.
steps.detail: A binary search on unsorted data does not error: it returns absent, or the wrong index, quietly. Either sort first — paying O(n log n) once, which is worth it across many searches — or scan linearly. Deciding which depends on how many searches there will be.
steps.proof: The search reports something demonstrably wrong, and you can say why.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a binary search's answer on data nobody checked was sorted.

problems.prompt: Binary search [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] for 4. What is wrong with the answer?
problems.answer: It may report absent — the halving is invalid on unsorted data.

problems.prompt: You will search a 1000-element list 500 times. Sort first or scan each time?
problems.answer: Sort once, then 500 searches of about 10 comparisons each.

problems.prompt: You will search it twice. Which is cheaper?
problems.answer: Two linear scans, since the sort costs more than it saves.

steps.title: Build a Set
steps.mastery: Create a set from a sequence and see the duplicates disappear.
steps.practice: Build a set from [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3] and print its size.
steps.detail: A set stores each value once, so the size is the count of distinct values rather than of elements. Print both len of the list and len of the set to see 6 against 3. Order is not preserved, so never rely on the order a set prints in.
steps.proof: The list has 6 elements and the set has 3.
steps.pitfall: Expecting a set to keep insertion order, then relying on the first element printed.

problems.prompt: What is the size of the set built from [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]?
How many distinct values are in [4, 4, 4, 4]?
Can you rely on set([3, 1, 2]) printing in the order 3, 1, 2?
problems.answer: No — a set does not preserve order.

steps.title: Test Membership Fast
steps.mastery: Check whether a value is present in roughly constant time.
steps.practice: Test whether 9999 is in a list of 10000 numbers and in a set of the same, and time both.
steps.detail: A list membership test scans until it finds the value, so a miss costs n comparisons; a set hashes the value and looks in one place, which is O(1). The timing difference is small at 100 elements and obvious at 100,000, so use the larger size if the difference does not show.
steps.proof: Both report True, and the set test is the faster of the 2.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a list because the data is small, then using it inside a loop, which turns O(n) into O(n^2).

problems.prompt: Scanning a list of 10000 numbers for a value that is absent costs how many comparisons?
problems.answer: 10000 — one per element.

problems.prompt: A set hashes the value and looks in 1 place. What order is that?
problems.answer: O(1) on average.

problems.prompt: A loop over 10000 items tests membership in a 10000-element list each time. What is the total order?
problems.answer: O(n^2) — about 100 million comparisons.

steps.title: Intersect and Subtract
steps.mastery: Combine two sets with the standard operations.
steps.practice: For A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}, give the union, intersection and A minus B.
steps.detail: Union is everything in either, intersection is what is in both, and difference is order-sensitive: A minus B is not B minus A. Work all 4 out by hand before running them, because the one people get wrong is the direction of the difference.
steps.proof: Union {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, intersection {3, 4}, A minus B {1, 2}.
steps.pitfall: Assuming A minus B equals B minus A, which here is {1, 2} against {5}.

problems.prompt: Which values are in both {2, 6, 9} and {6, 9, 11}?
problems.answer: 6 and 9.

problems.prompt: Subtracting B = {3, 4, 5} from A = {1, 2, 3, 4} leaves what, and reversing the direction leaves what?
How many elements are in the union of those 2 sets?

steps.title: Deduplicate a List
steps.mastery: Remove repeats from a sequence, with and without keeping order.
steps.practice: Deduplicate [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] both ways and print the 2 results.
steps.detail: Converting to a set and back loses the order; keeping order needs a set for the seen values and a list for the output, appending only when the value is new. The second is still one pass, because the membership test is O(1).
steps.proof: The order-preserving version gives [3, 1, 2].
steps.pitfall: Checking the output list for membership instead of a set, which makes the pass O(n^2).

problems.prompt: Deduplicate [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] preserving order. What is the result?
Why keep a separate set of seen values rather than testing the output list of 5 items?
problems.answer: The set test is O(1), so the pass stays O(n) instead of becoming O(n^2).

problems.prompt: What does set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) lose?
problems.answer: The original order of the 3 distinct values.

steps.title: Find the Common Elements
steps.mastery: Use a set to answer an overlap question in one pass.
steps.practice: Given [1, 3, 5, 7] and [5, 7, 9], find the common values without a nested loop.
steps.detail: Put the smaller sequence in a set, then walk the other testing membership. That is n + m work rather than n times m, which is the standard reason a set appears in a solution. Print the result sorted so the answer is stable.
steps.proof: You get [5, 7], found in 1 pass over each list.
steps.pitfall: Writing the nested loop first because it is 2 lines, then keeping it when the inputs grow.

problems.prompt: Find the common values of [1, 3, 5, 7] and [5, 7, 9].
problems.answer: 5 and 7.

problems.prompt: A nested loop compares every element of a 4-item list with every element of a 3-item list. What order is that?
problems.answer: O(n times m).

problems.prompt: Putting 3 items in a set and walking the other 4 costs what order?
problems.answer: O(n + m).

steps.title: Know What Cannot Go In
steps.mastery: Say which values a set can hold and why.
steps.practice: Try adding the list [1, 2] to a set, then the tuple (1, 2), and note which works.
steps.detail: A set needs its members hashable, which in practice means immutable: numbers, strings and tuples are fine, lists and dictionaries are not. The reason is that a set finds a value by its hash, and a value whose contents can change would move without telling the set.
steps.proof: The tuple is accepted and the list raises TypeError: unhashable type.
steps.pitfall: Trying to build a set of lists to deduplicate rows, which fails and needs tuples instead.

problems.prompt: Which can go in a set: the list [1, 2] or the tuple (1, 2)?
problems.answer: The tuple — a list is unhashable.

problems.prompt: Why must a member of a set of 3 values be immutable?
problems.answer: The set locates it by its hash, which would change if the contents could.

problems.prompt: You want to deduplicate 100 rows held as lists. What is the fix?
problems.answer: Convert each row to a tuple before putting it in the set.

steps.title: Sum a Fixed Window
steps.mastery: Total every window of a fixed size in one pass.
steps.practice: Find the largest sum of 3 consecutive values in [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2].
steps.detail: Sum the first 3, then slide: add the entering value and subtract the leaving one. That keeps each step O(1) instead of re-summing 3 values, which is the whole idea. The best window here is 5, 1, 3.
steps.proof: The largest sum is 9.
steps.pitfall: Re-summing the window at each position, which is O(n times k) and defeats the technique.

problems.prompt: Largest sum of 3 consecutive values in [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]?
How many windows of size 3 does a 6-element array have?
What 2 operations move the window by 1 position?
problems.answer: Add the entering value and subtract the leaving one.

steps.title: Grow and Shrink
steps.mastery: Vary a window's size to satisfy a condition.
steps.practice: Find the shortest run in [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] summing to 7 or more.
steps.detail: Extend the right edge until the condition holds, then pull the left edge in while it still holds, recording the best length. Each index enters and leaves once, so the pass is O(n) even though the window changes size. The answer here is 4, 3 with length 2.
steps.proof: The shortest qualifying run has length 2.
steps.pitfall: Restarting the window from each left position, which is the O(n^2) version.

problems.prompt: Shortest run in [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] summing to at least 7?
problems.answer: Length 2, from 4 and 3.

problems.prompt: How many times does each of the 6 indices enter and leave the window?
problems.answer: Once each, which keeps the pass O(n).

problems.prompt: When does the left edge of a window over 6 elements move in?
problems.answer: While the condition still holds after shrinking.

steps.title: Window With a Map
steps.mastery: Track the contents of a window, not just its total.
steps.practice: Find the longest substring of "abcabcbb" with no repeated character.
steps.detail: Hold a map of character to its last index. When a repeat enters the window, move the left edge past that character's previous position rather than by 1. The answer is 3, from "abc", and the map is what makes the left jump correct in one step.
steps.proof: The longest run is 3 characters.
steps.pitfall: Moving the left edge by 1 on a repeat, which is correct but degrades to O(n^2) in the worst case.

problems.prompt: Longest substring of "abcabcbb" with no repeat?
problems.answer: 3, such as "abc".

problems.prompt: Longest substring of "bbbbb" with no repeat?
Where does the left edge jump to when a repeat enters a window over "abcabcbb"?
problems.answer: One past that character's previous index.

steps.title: Count Inside the Window
steps.mastery: Maintain a tally as elements enter and leave.
steps.practice: Count how many windows of 4 in "aabacbeb" hold exactly 2 distinct letters.
steps.detail: Increment the entering character's count and decrement the leaving one, deleting the key when it reaches 0 so the distinct count is just the map's size. Forgetting the delete is why a window reports more distinct characters than it holds.
steps.proof: You can state the count and show the map's size for each window.
steps.pitfall: Leaving zero-count keys in the map, which inflates the distinct count.

problems.prompt: Why delete a key when its count reaches 0 in a window of 4?
problems.answer: Otherwise the map's size overstates the distinct characters.

problems.prompt: What 2 updates happen when the window slides 1 position?
problems.answer: The entering character's count goes up and the leaving one's goes down.

problems.prompt: How do you read the number of distinct characters from a map of 4 counts?
problems.answer: It is the map's size, once zero-count keys are removed.

steps.title: Handle the Empty Answer
steps.mastery: Return the right thing when no window qualifies.
steps.practice: Run the shortest-run search on [1, 1, 1] with a target of 7 and return 0 rather than a length.
steps.detail: Initialise the best length to something impossible — infinity or n + 1 — and convert it to 0 at the end if it never improved. Initialising to 0 instead makes an unsatisfiable input look like a perfect answer, which is a bug that only appears on inputs nobody tests.
steps.proof: The search returns 0 for [1, 1, 1] with target 7.
steps.pitfall: Initialising the best length to 0, so the impossible case reports success.

problems.prompt: What should the shortest-run search return on [1, 1, 1] with a target of 7?
problems.answer: 0, since no window qualifies.

problems.prompt: What do you initialise the best length to on an array of 3, and why?
problems.answer: Infinity or n + 1, so an unimproved value is detectable.

problems.prompt: What does initialising the best length to 0 make the impossible case look like?
problems.answer: A successful answer of length 0.

steps.title: Fixed Versus Variable
steps.mastery: Tell which kind of window a problem asks for.
steps.practice: Label these 2 as fixed or variable: average of every 5 consecutive readings, longest run under a limit.
steps.detail: If the size is given, the window is fixed and the loop is simple. If the size is what you are solving for, it is variable and needs the grow-shrink pair. Mixing them up produces a loop that either never shrinks or never holds its promised size.
steps.proof: The 5-reading average is fixed; the longest run is variable.
steps.pitfall: Writing a fixed-size loop for a variable-size question, which cannot find a length it was told to assume.

problems.prompt: Average of every 5 consecutive readings: fixed or variable window?
problems.answer: Fixed.

problems.prompt: Longest run summing under 100: fixed or variable?
problems.answer: Variable — the length is the answer.

problems.prompt: What does a variable window need that a fixed one of size 5 does not?
problems.answer: A shrink step on the left edge.

steps.title: Prove the Linear Bound
steps.mastery: Explain why a grow-shrink loop is O(n) despite the nested look.
steps.practice: Count the total pointer moves for the shortest-run search over 6 elements and compare with 6 squared.
steps.detail: The inner shrink looks like a nested loop but the left pointer only ever moves forward, so across the whole run it moves at most n times — 12 moves in total for 6 elements, not 36. Being able to say that is what stops you rewriting a correct O(n) solution because it looked quadratic.
steps.proof: At most 12 pointer moves against 36 for the quadratic version.
steps.pitfall: Calling the grow-shrink loop O(n^2) because there is a loop inside a loop.

problems.prompt: How many times can the left pointer move across a run over 6 elements?
problems.answer: At most 6.

problems.prompt: Total pointer moves for both edges over 6 elements?
problems.answer: At most 12.

problems.prompt: Why is a loop inside a loop not always O(n^2)?
problems.answer: Here the inner pointer never resets, so the total work is bounded by n.

steps.title: Sort by Comparison
steps.mastery: Order a list and control the comparison used.
steps.practice: Sort [5, 2, 9, 1] ascending, then sort ["pear", "fig", "apple"] by length.
steps.detail: A library sort takes a key function, which is how you sort by something other than the value itself. Sorting by length gives fig, pear, apple. Note whether your sort returns a new list or reorders in place, because using the return value of an in-place sort gives None.
steps.proof: You get [1, 2, 5, 9] and fig, pear, apple.
steps.pitfall: Assigning the result of an in-place sort, which leaves you holding None.

problems.prompt: Sort [5, 2, 9, 1] ascending.
Sort ["pear", "fig", "apple"] by length.
problems.answer: fig, pear, apple.

problems.prompt: x = items.sort() leaves x as what, in Python?
problems.answer: None — the sort works in place.

steps.title: Sort a Small Array by Hand
steps.mastery: Carry out one simple sorting algorithm step by step.
steps.practice: Run insertion sort on [4, 2, 5, 1] writing the array after each of the 3 insertions.
steps.detail: Take each element and slide it left past everything larger. Writing the intermediate arrays is the point — [4], [2, 4], [2, 4, 5], [1, 2, 4, 5] — because it shows why the cost is quadratic on reversed input and linear on nearly sorted input.
steps.proof: The 3 intermediate states end at [1, 2, 4, 5].
steps.pitfall: Sliding the element without shifting the larger ones right, which overwrites values.

problems.prompt: Insertion sort [4, 2, 5, 1]. What is the array after the 2nd insertion?
What input makes insertion sort O(n) rather than O(n^2)?
problems.answer: An already sorted or nearly sorted array.

problems.prompt: What is insertion sort's cost on a reversed array of 4 elements?
problems.answer: The worst case, 6 comparisons — O(n^2) in general.

steps.title: Merge Sort in Two Halves
steps.mastery: Split, sort each half and merge the results.
steps.practice: Merge sort [3, 1, 4, 2] by hand, writing the 2 halves and the merge that joins them.
steps.detail: Split to single elements, then merge pairs back. The merge is the two-pointer walk from the earlier topic, which is why that step is worth having first. The recursion depth is log2(4) = 2 and each level does n work, giving n log n.
steps.proof: You get [1, 2, 3, 4], with 2 levels of merging.
steps.pitfall: Merging without a stable comparison, which reorders equal elements for no reason.

problems.prompt: How many levels of splitting does merge sort make on 4 elements?
problems.answer: 2, since log2(4) is 2.

problems.prompt: How much work does each of the 2 merge levels do?
problems.answer: O(n) — every element is touched once per level.

problems.prompt: What is merge sort's order overall?
problems.answer: O(n log n).

steps.title: Know the n log n Floor
steps.mastery: Say why no comparison sort can beat n log n in general.
steps.practice: Work out how many orderings 4 elements have, and how many yes-or-no comparisons are needed to single one out.
steps.detail: Four elements have 4 factorial = 24 orderings, and each comparison at best halves the possibilities, so you need at least log2(24), about 5 comparisons. Generalised, log2(n factorial) is about n log n, which is the floor. Counting sorts beat it by not comparing at all.
steps.proof: 24 orderings and about 5 comparisons minimum.
steps.pitfall: Quoting the floor as a law for all sorting, when counting and radix sorts are not comparison sorts.

problems.prompt: How many orderings do 4 distinct elements have?
At best, what does 1 comparison do to the number of remaining possibilities?
problems.answer: Halves it.

problems.prompt: Name 1 sort that beats n log n, and why it is allowed to.
problems.answer: Counting sort — it does not compare elements, so the bound does not apply.

steps.title: Sort by a Key
steps.mastery: Order records by one field, then by a second.
steps.practice: Sort 4 name-and-score pairs by score descending, breaking ties by name ascending.
steps.detail: Most libraries sort stably, so you can sort by the secondary key first and then by the primary — or pass a tuple key with the descending field negated. Write out the expected order before running it, because a tie is where the 2 approaches differ visibly.
steps.proof: The 4 pairs come out in score order with the tied pair alphabetical.
steps.pitfall: Sorting by the primary key first and then by the secondary, which discards the primary order.

problems.prompt: To sort by score descending then name ascending in 2 passes, which key goes first?
problems.answer: Name ascending first, then score descending, relying on stability.

problems.prompt: What does a stable sort guarantee about 2 records with equal scores?
problems.answer: They keep their previous relative order.

problems.prompt: Give a single tuple key for score descending and name ascending, using 4 pairs.
problems.answer: (-score, name).

steps.title: Sort as a Preprocessing Step
steps.mastery: Use a sort to make a later pass simple.
steps.practice: Find the 2 closest values in [8, 3, 15, 1, 9] by sorting first, and give the pair.
steps.detail: Once sorted, the closest pair must be adjacent, so a single pass over 4 gaps finds it — O(n log n) total against O(n^2) for comparing all pairs. Recognising that a sort turns a quadratic problem linear is most of what sorting is for in practice.
steps.proof: The closest pair is 8 and 9, found in 1 pass after sorting.
steps.pitfall: Comparing all 10 pairs when sorting first reduces it to 4 comparisons.

problems.prompt: What is the closest pair in [8, 3, 15, 1, 9]?
problems.answer: 8 and 9.

problems.prompt: Why must the closest pair be adjacent once 5 values are sorted?
problems.answer: Any non-adjacent pair is at least as far apart as the gaps between them.

problems.prompt: How many comparisons does the sorted pass need over 5 elements, against all pairs?
problems.answer: 4 against 10.

steps.title: Choose the Right Sort
steps.mastery: Pick a sorting approach from the data's properties.
steps.practice: Say which approach suits each: 10 nearly sorted values, 1 million integers from 0 to 100, sorting with 0 extra memory.
steps.detail: Nearly sorted wants insertion sort, which is O(n) there. A million small integers want counting sort, which is O(n) by not comparing. No extra memory wants heapsort or an in-place quicksort, since merge sort needs O(n). The library sort is the right answer when none of these apply, which is most of the time.
steps.proof: Insertion, counting and heapsort respectively, each for a stated reason.
steps.pitfall: Reaching for a hand-written sort when the library's is faster and already correct.

problems.prompt: Which sort suits 1 million integers ranging 0 to 100?
problems.answer: Counting sort — O(n) with a fixed range.

problems.prompt: Which suits 10 nearly sorted values?
problems.answer: Insertion sort, which is O(n) on nearly sorted input.

problems.prompt: Which of merge sort and heapsort needs O(n) extra memory?
problems.answer: Merge sort.

steps.title: Push and Pop
steps.mastery: Use a stack so the last item in is the first out.
steps.practice: Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, pop twice, and say what remains.
steps.detail: A list makes a fine stack: append to push and pop with no argument to take the last. Write the 3 pushes and 2 pops out on paper first — the answer is that 3 and then 2 come off, leaving 1 — then check it in code.
steps.proof: The pops return 3 and 2, leaving [1].
steps.pitfall: Using pop(0), which takes from the wrong end and turns the stack into a queue.

problems.prompt: Push 1, 2, 3 then pop twice. What comes off, in order?
problems.answer: 3, then 2.

problems.prompt: What remains on the stack after those 2 pops?
problems.answer: Just 1.

problems.prompt: What does pop(0) do to a list used as a stack?
problems.answer: Takes from the front, making it behave as a queue instead.

steps.title: Match the Brackets
steps.mastery: Check a string's brackets with a stack.
steps.practice: Test "([]{})" and "([)]" for balanced brackets using a stack.
steps.detail: Push every opening bracket; on a closing bracket pop and check the pair matches. Two failure conditions: a mismatch when popping, and a non-empty stack at the end. The second string fails on the mismatch, which is what a simple counter cannot catch.
steps.proof: The first is balanced and the second is not.
steps.pitfall: Counting openers and closers instead of stacking them, which calls "([)]" balanced.

problems.prompt: Is "([)]" balanced, and what detects the fault?
problems.answer: No — popping on the ) finds a [ rather than a (.

problems.prompt: What does a non-empty stack at the end of a scan of 6 characters mean?
problems.answer: There are unclosed opening brackets.

problems.prompt: Why does counting 3 openers and 3 closers not settle it?
problems.answer: A count ignores order, so "([)]" passes wrongly.

steps.title: Enqueue and Dequeue
steps.mastery: Use a queue so the first item in is the first out.
steps.practice: Enqueue 1, 2, 3 then dequeue twice, and say what remains.
steps.detail: First in, first out: 1 and then 2 come off. Taking from the front of a plain list is O(n) because everything shifts, so use a deque for anything with 1000 or more operations. The interface is the same; the cost is not.
steps.proof: The dequeues return 1 and 2, leaving 3.
steps.pitfall: Using list.pop(0) in a loop over 100,000 items, which is quietly O(n^2).

problems.prompt: Enqueue 1, 2, 3 then dequeue twice. What comes off?
problems.answer: 1, then 2.

problems.prompt: What is the cost of list.pop(0) on a list of n elements?
problems.answer: O(n), because every remaining element shifts down.

problems.prompt: What should hold a queue of 100,000 operations?
problems.answer: A deque, which removes from the front in O(1).

steps.title: Reverse With a Stack
steps.mastery: Use last-in-first-out to invert an order.
steps.practice: Reverse the string "stack" by pushing every character and popping them all.
steps.detail: Push all 5 characters, then pop until empty and join the results. This is the cheapest demonstration that a stack reverses order, and it is the mechanism behind undo, backtracking and the call stack unwinding.
steps.proof: You get "kcats".
steps.pitfall: Popping while still pushing, which interleaves the 2 and reverses nothing.

problems.prompt: Reverse "stack" with a stack. What is the output?
problems.answer: "kcats".

problems.prompt: Why must all 5 pushes happen before any pop?
problems.answer: Interleaving pushes and pops does not reverse the order.

problems.prompt: Name 1 real mechanism that relies on a stack reversing order.
problems.answer: Undo in an editor, or the call stack unwinding.

steps.title: Two Stacks, One Queue
steps.mastery: Build first-in-first-out behaviour from 2 last-in-first-out structures.
steps.practice: Implement a queue with 2 stacks, then enqueue 1, 2, 3 and dequeue once.
steps.detail: Push arrivals onto stack A. To dequeue, if stack B is empty pour all of A into B — which reverses the order — then pop B. Each item moves at most twice, so the average cost is O(1) even though a single dequeue can be O(n).
steps.proof: The first dequeue returns 1.
steps.pitfall: Pouring A into B when B still has items, which puts the newer arrivals in front of the older ones.

problems.prompt: In the 2-stack queue, when may stack A be poured into stack B?
problems.answer: Only when B is empty.

problems.prompt: After enqueueing 1, 2, 3, what does the first dequeue return?
How many times does an item move between the 2 stacks?
problems.answer: At most twice, giving O(1) amortised cost.

steps.title: Pick the Discipline
steps.mastery: Decide whether a problem wants a stack or a queue.
steps.practice: Label these 4 as stack or queue: undo history, print jobs, depth-first search, breadth-first search.
steps.detail: Ask what should come out next. If it is the most recent thing — undo, nested brackets, depth-first — that is a stack. If it is the thing that has waited longest — print jobs, breadth-first, fair scheduling — that is a queue. The graph searches differ only in this choice.
steps.proof: Undo and depth-first are stacks; print jobs and breadth-first are queues.
steps.pitfall: Using a stack for a breadth-first search, which silently makes it depth-first.

problems.prompt: Stack or queue for a breadth-first search over 20 nodes?
problems.answer: A queue.

problems.prompt: Stack or queue for an undo history of 20 actions?
problems.answer: A stack — the most recent action comes off first.

problems.prompt: What is the only structural difference between depth-first and breadth-first search over 20 nodes?
problems.answer: Whether the pending nodes are held on a stack or in a queue.

steps.title: Index and Slice
steps.mastery: Take characters and substrings out of a string by position.
steps.practice: From "algorithm", print character 0, characters 2 to 5, and the last 3 characters.
steps.detail: A slice runs from the start index up to but not including the end, so 2 to 5 gives 3 characters. Negative indices count from the end, and s[-3:] is the last 3. Check the length first so the off-by-one is visible rather than guessed.
steps.proof: You print a, gor and thm.
steps.pitfall: Expecting s[2:5] to include character 5, which it never does.

problems.prompt: What does "algorithm"[2:5] return?
problems.answer: "gor".

problems.prompt: How many characters does the slice s[4:9] contain?
Write the slice for the last 3 characters of a string s.

steps.title: Reverse a String
steps.mastery: Produce a string's characters in the opposite order.
steps.practice: Reverse "stressed" two ways: with a slice, and with a loop that builds the result.
steps.detail: The slice s[::-1] is the idiom; the loop is worth writing once so the mechanism is not magic. Walk from len(s) - 1 down to 0 and append each character. Reversing "stressed" gives a real word, which makes the check obvious.
steps.proof: Both give "desserts".
steps.pitfall: Looping from len(s) down to 0, which starts one past the end.

problems.prompt: What is "stressed" reversed?
problems.answer: "desserts".

problems.prompt: A reversing loop starting at len(s) raises IndexError. What is the first valid index?
problems.answer: len(s) - 1.

problems.prompt: What does s[::-1] do?
problems.answer: Returns the string with its characters in reverse order.

steps.title: Count Characters
steps.mastery: Tally the occurrences of each character in a string.
steps.practice: Count the letters in "mississippi" and report the tally for i, s and p.
steps.detail: Use a dictionary keyed by character, adding 1 for each. Handle the first sighting of a character explicitly — either check membership or use a default — because incrementing a key that does not exist is the error here. Case matters unless you lower the string first.
steps.proof: You get i:4, s:4, p:2.
steps.pitfall: Incrementing counts[c] before the key exists, which raises KeyError.

problems.prompt: How many times does s appear in "mississippi"?
A tally raises KeyError on the first sighting of a character. What is missing?
problems.answer: A default of 0, or a membership check before incrementing.

problems.prompt: Counting "Apple" gives A:1 and a:0. What was not done?
problems.answer: The string was not lower-cased before counting.

steps.title: Test for a Palindrome
steps.mastery: Decide whether a string reads the same both ways.
steps.practice: Test "racecar", "Racecar" and "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" for palindromes.
steps.detail: Compare the string with its reverse, but normalise first: lower the case and strip anything that is not a letter or digit. The third example is a palindrome only after normalising, which is the whole point of including it.
steps.proof: All 3 report true once case and punctuation are stripped.
steps.pitfall: Comparing raw strings, which calls "Racecar" not a palindrome because R and r differ.

problems.prompt: Is "Racecar" a palindrome by a raw comparison, and after lower-casing?
problems.answer: No raw, yes after lower-casing.

problems.prompt: What 2 normalisations does "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" need?
problems.answer: Lower-casing, and stripping non-alphanumeric characters.

problems.prompt: Is "ab" a palindrome?
problems.answer: No — reversed it is "ba".

steps.title: Split and Join
steps.mastery: Break a string into parts and rebuild it from them.
steps.practice: Split "one,two,,three" on commas, count the parts, then join them with a hyphen.
steps.detail: Splitting on a delimiter keeps empty fields, so this gives 4 parts and not 3 — which is the behaviour that catches people parsing CSV by hand. Join is the inverse, called on the separator with the list as its argument.
steps.proof: You get 4 parts and "one-two--three".
steps.pitfall: Assuming a split drops empty fields, so a 4-field line silently becomes 3.

problems.prompt: How many parts does "one,two,,three" split into on a comma?
problems.answer: 4, including an empty string.

problems.prompt: Join ["a", "b", "c"] with a hyphen. What is the result?
Splitting a line of 5 comma-separated fields where 2 are blank gives how many parts?
problems.answer: 5 — blank fields are kept.

steps.title: Build a Small Tree
steps.mastery: Define a node with children and assemble a tree from it.
steps.practice: Build a 3-level binary tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and leaves 4 and 5 under 2.
steps.detail: A node holds a value and references to left and right, either of which may be None. The root is the only entry point, so keep it. Draw the tree on paper alongside the code, because almost every later bug is a mismatch between the drawing and the links.
steps.proof: The root's left child holds 2, whose children are 4 and 5.
steps.pitfall: Losing the root reference while building, which leaves a tree nobody can reach.

problems.prompt: How many nodes does the tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, and leaves 4 and 5 hold?
What are the 3 fields of a binary tree node?
problems.answer: A value, a left child and a right child.

problems.prompt: How many leaves does that 5-node tree have?
problems.answer: 3 — nodes 3, 4 and 5.

steps.title: Walk It Three Ways
steps.mastery: Produce pre-order, in-order and post-order traversals.
steps.practice: Give all 3 traversals of the tree with root 1, left 2 with leaves 4 and 5, and right 3.
steps.detail: The names say when the node is visited relative to its children: pre-order is node, left, right; in-order is left, node, right; post-order is left, right, node. All 3 are the same 3 lines of recursion with the visit moved.
steps.proof: Pre-order 1 2 4 5 3, in-order 4 2 5 1 3, post-order 4 5 2 3 1.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up in-order and pre-order, which only differ visibly once a node has a left child.

problems.prompt: Give the in-order traversal of that 5-node tree.
Give the post-order traversal of that 5-node tree.
What distinguishes the 3 traversals in code?
problems.answer: Where the visit sits relative to the 2 recursive calls.

steps.title: Measure the Height
steps.mastery: Compute a tree's depth recursively.
steps.practice: Find the height of a tree whose root has 1 child with 1 child, and of a single node.
steps.detail: Height is 1 plus the larger of the 2 subtree heights, with an empty subtree counting 0. So a chain of 3 has height 3 and a lone node has height 1. Decide whether you count nodes or edges and say so, because the 2 conventions differ by 1 and both appear in textbooks.
steps.proof: Heights of 3 and 1, counting nodes.
steps.pitfall: Returning 0 for a single node while the rest of the code counts nodes, which puts every height out by 1.

problems.prompt: What is the height of a chain of 3 nodes, counting nodes?
A tree of 1 node has what height, counting nodes rather than edges?
What does the height recursion return for an empty subtree — 0 or 1?

steps.title: Search Breadth First
steps.mastery: Visit a tree level by level with a queue.
steps.practice: Print the 5-node tree level by level and say which structure holds the pending nodes.
steps.detail: Start with the root in a queue; pop a node, print it, push its children. The queue is what makes it level order — swap in a stack and it becomes depth-first. Level order gives 1, then 2 and 3, then 4 and 5.
steps.proof: The output is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the pending nodes sit in a queue.
steps.pitfall: Using a stack and reporting the result as a level-order traversal.

problems.prompt: Give the level order of the tree with root 1, left 2 with leaves 4 and 5, right 3.
Which structure holds the pending nodes in a breadth-first walk of 5?
problems.answer: A queue.

problems.prompt: Replace that queue with a stack. What have you built?
problems.answer: A depth-first traversal.

steps.title: Count Nodes and Leaves
steps.mastery: Aggregate over a tree by combining subtree results.
steps.practice: Count the nodes and then the leaves of the 5-node tree with 1 recursion each.
steps.detail: Nodes is 1 plus both subtree counts; leaves is the sum of the subtree leaf counts, or 1 when both children are None. Defining the leaf base case correctly is the only difficulty: an empty subtree has 0 leaves, not 1.
steps.proof: 5 nodes and 3 leaves.
steps.pitfall: Returning 1 for an empty subtree in the leaf count, which double-counts every node with 1 child.

problems.prompt: How many leaves does the tree with root 1, left 2 with leaves 4 and 5, right 3 have?
How many leaves does an empty subtree have — 0 or 1?
What is the node count expression in terms of the 2 subtrees?
problems.answer: 1 plus the left count plus the right count.

steps.title: Handle the Empty Tree
steps.mastery: Make every tree function correct on no nodes at all.
steps.practice: Call your height, count and traversal functions on an empty tree and check all 3 return sensibly.
steps.detail: An empty tree is the base case of every tree recursion, and a function that assumes a root exists fails on it — usually with an attribute error rather than a wrong answer. Height 0, count 0 and an empty traversal list are the 3 right answers.
steps.proof: Height 0, count 0 and an empty traversal, with no exception.
steps.pitfall: Checking the children for None but never the node itself, so the top-level empty case raises.

problems.prompt: What should height, count and traversal return for a tree of 0 nodes?
problems.answer: 0, 0 and an empty list.

problems.prompt: Why does an unhandled tree of 0 nodes raise rather than return a wrong value?
problems.answer: The code reads an attribute of None.

problems.prompt: Which case is the base case of nearly every tree recursion — 0 nodes or 1?
problems.answer: The empty tree.

steps.title: Compare Two Trees
steps.mastery: Decide whether two trees have the same shape and values.
steps.practice: Write a recursion comparing 2 trees and test it on an identical pair and on a mirrored pair.
steps.detail: Both empty is true, one empty is false, otherwise values must match and both subtree comparisons must hold. The mirrored pair is the test that matters: it has the same values and the same shape reflected, and a comparison that ignores side reports it as equal.
steps.proof: The identical pair reports true and the mirrored pair false.
steps.pitfall: Comparing sorted traversals, which calls 2 differently shaped trees equal.

problems.prompt: Both trees are empty. Equal or not?
problems.answer: Equal.

problems.prompt: One tree is the mirror of the other, with the same 5 values. Equal?
problems.answer: No — left and right differ.

problems.prompt: Why is comparing 2 sorted traversals of 5 values wrong?
problems.answer: Different shapes can produce the same multiset of values.

steps.title: Recognise a Tree Problem
steps.mastery: Spot when data is a tree and which walk it wants.
steps.practice: Say which walk suits each of these 3: an indented folder listing, the shallowest match, an expression tree.
steps.detail: Indented output and expression evaluation are depth-first, because a node's result depends on its children. The shallowest match wants breadth-first, because the first match found is then the nearest. Getting this the wrong way round makes a correct algorithm slow rather than wrong.
steps.proof: Depth-first, breadth-first, depth-first, each with a reason.
steps.pitfall: Using depth-first for a shallowest-match search, which may explore a long branch before finding a near answer.

problems.prompt: Finding the shallowest node matching a condition: which of the 2 walks?
problems.answer: Breadth-first.

problems.prompt: Evaluating an expression tree of 7 nodes: which walk?
problems.answer: Depth-first, post-order, since a node needs its children's values.

problems.prompt: Why is depth-first a poor choice when the match is 2 levels down a 40-level tree?
problems.answer: It can explore a deep branch before reaching a near match.

steps.title: One Node per Character
steps.mastery: Store a word as a path of characters through a tree.
steps.practice: Insert "cat" into an empty trie and say how many nodes the path adds.
steps.detail: Each node holds a map from character to child, and a word is the path from the root. Inserting "cat" adds 3 nodes below the root. The root itself holds no character, which is the part people draw wrongly.
steps.proof: 3 nodes below the root, spelling c, a, t.
steps.pitfall: Storing the whole word at each node, which is a tree of strings rather than a trie.

problems.prompt: Inserting "cat" into an empty trie adds how many nodes?
What character does the root node of a 3-node path hold?
problems.answer: None — it is the empty prefix.

problems.prompt: What does each of the 3 nodes map from and to?
problems.answer: A character to a child node.

steps.title: Share the Prefix
steps.mastery: Insert words so common prefixes are stored once.
steps.practice: Insert "car", "cart" and "cat" and count the total nodes below the root.
steps.detail: "car" adds 3, "cart" adds 1 more, and "cat" adds 1 — 5 nodes for 10 characters of input. That sharing is the whole point: a dictionary of 100,000 English words has far fewer nodes than characters.
steps.proof: 5 nodes hold all 3 words.
steps.pitfall: Creating a fresh path per word, which is a list of words with extra pointers.

problems.prompt: How many nodes below the root hold "car", "cart" and "cat"?
How many characters are in those 3 words in total, and how many nodes?
problems.answer: 10 characters, 5 nodes.

problems.prompt: Which node do "car" and "cat" share besides the root?
problems.answer: The c, and then they diverge at a and a.

steps.title: Mark the Word Ends
steps.mastery: Distinguish a stored word from a prefix of one.
steps.practice: With "cart" stored, test whether "car" is a stored word and whether it is a prefix.
steps.detail: Each node carries a flag saying whether a word ends there. Without it, "car" looks stored because its path exists. With "cart" alone, "car" is a prefix and not a word, and that distinction is what the flag exists for.
steps.proof: "car" reports as a prefix and not as a stored word.
steps.pitfall: Treating any reachable path as a word, which returns true for every prefix in the trie.

problems.prompt: With only "cart" stored, is "car" a stored word?
problems.answer: No — it is a prefix.

problems.prompt: Is "car" a prefix in that trie?
problems.answer: Yes.

problems.prompt: What does each node need besides its 26 possible children?
problems.answer: A flag saying whether a word ends there.

steps.title: Search and Prefix Search
steps.mastery: Answer both exact and prefix questions with one walk.
steps.practice: With "car", "cart" and "cat" stored, search for "cap" and for the prefix "ca".
steps.detail: Walk the characters; if a child is missing the answer is no. "cap" fails at p, while "ca" succeeds as a prefix. Both cost the length of the query rather than the size of the dictionary, which is what a trie buys over a list.
steps.proof: "cap" is absent and "ca" is a valid prefix.
steps.pitfall: Quoting the cost as O(n) in the number of words, when it is O(k) in the query length.

problems.prompt: Searching "cap" in a trie of "car", "cart", "cat" fails at which character?
problems.answer: The p.

problems.prompt: What does a lookup cost in terms of a query of length 3?
problems.answer: O(k), independent of how many words are stored.

problems.prompt: Is "ca" a valid prefix in that trie?
problems.answer: Yes.

steps.title: List What Follows a Prefix
steps.mastery: Collect every word under a given prefix.
steps.practice: List all words under the prefix "ca" in a trie holding "car", "cart", "cat" and "dog".
steps.detail: Walk to the prefix node, then explore everything below it, collecting at each end-of-word flag. That gives car, cart and cat, and never touches the d branch. This is exactly what an autocomplete does, and why a trie is the structure behind one.
steps.proof: 3 words come back and the "dog" branch is never visited.
steps.pitfall: Scanning every word and testing startswith, which is the O(n) version a trie exists to replace.

problems.prompt: Which words sit under the prefix "ca" in a trie of "car", "cart", "cat", "dog"?
problems.answer: car, cart and cat.

problems.prompt: How many of the 4 branches does the walk visit?
problems.answer: 1 — the c branch only.

problems.prompt: Which feature is listing the 3 words under a prefix the basis of?
problems.answer: Autocomplete.

steps.title: Count the Memory
steps.mastery: State what a trie costs in space and when that hurts.
steps.practice: Work out how many child slots a fixed-array trie node needs for lowercase English, and compare with a map.
steps.detail: A fixed array of 26 pointers per node is fast and wasteful: most nodes have 1 or 2 children, so 24 slots sit empty. A map per node saves memory and costs a hash per step. For 26 letters the array usually wins; for Unicode it never does.
steps.proof: 26 slots per node against 1 or 2 used, and a reason to prefer each layout.
steps.pitfall: Using a 26-slot array for Unicode text, which allocates thousands of empty pointers per node.

problems.prompt: How many child slots does a fixed-array node need for lowercase English?
Most nodes use how many of the 26 slots?
problems.answer: 1 or 2.

problems.prompt: Which layout suits Unicode text, and why?
problems.answer: A map per node — an array would allocate thousands of empty slots.

steps.title: Delete a Word
steps.mastery: Remove a word without breaking the words that share its path.
steps.practice: Delete "cart" from a trie holding "car" and "cart", and say which nodes go.
steps.detail: Clear the end-of-word flag, then remove nodes upwards only while they have no children and no flag. Here just the t goes, because the r ends "car". Removing the whole path is the bug, and it deletes a word nobody asked about.
steps.proof: Only the t node is removed and "car" still resolves.
steps.pitfall: Deleting the whole path for the word, which takes "car" with it.

problems.prompt: Delete "cart" from a trie holding "car" and "cart". Which nodes are removed?
problems.answer: Only the t.

problems.prompt: Under what 2 conditions may a node be removed upwards?
problems.answer: It has no children and no end-of-word flag.

problems.prompt: What breaks if the whole 4-node path is deleted?
problems.answer: "car" disappears too.

steps.title: Trie or Hash Set
steps.mastery: Decide when prefix structure is worth the memory.
steps.practice: Say which suits each of these 3: exact spell-check membership, autocomplete, finding the longest shared prefix of 1000 words.
steps.detail: A hash set wins exact membership on memory and speed. A trie wins anything about prefixes, because a hash set destroys the structure a prefix question needs. The longest shared prefix is the clearest case: a trie reads it off the path before the first branch.
steps.proof: Set, trie, trie, each with the reason.
steps.pitfall: Building a trie for plain membership testing, which pays a lot of memory for nothing.

problems.prompt: Exact membership for a 100,000-word spell-check: trie or hash set?
problems.answer: A hash set.

problems.prompt: Autocomplete over the same 100,000 words: which?
problems.answer: A trie.

problems.prompt: How does a trie give the longest common prefix of 1000 words?
problems.answer: It is the path from the root to the first node with more than 1 child.

steps.title: Walk From Both Ends
steps.mastery: Move two indices inward until they meet.
steps.practice: Check whether [1, 2, 3, 2, 1] is a palindrome using an index at each end.
steps.detail: Start left at 0 and right at n - 1, compare, then move both inward while left is less than right. That loop condition is the whole subtlety: less-than-or-equal compares the middle element with itself, which is harmless here and wrong in problems that move only one pointer.
steps.proof: The array reports as a palindrome after 2 comparisons.
steps.pitfall: Looping while left is not equal to right, which never terminates on an even-length array.

problems.prompt: How many comparisons does the 2-pointer check make on [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]?
Why does looping while left != right hang on a 4-element array?
problems.answer: The pointers cross without ever being equal.

problems.prompt: Where do left and right start on an array of 5 elements?
problems.answer: At 0 and 4.

steps.title: Pair Sum on Sorted Data
steps.mastery: Find a pair summing to a target in one pass over sorted input.
steps.practice: Find the pair in [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11] summing to 10 with 2 pointers.
steps.detail: If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if too large, move the right pointer left. Sortedness is what makes that decision sound, and it is why this beats the hash-map version when the input is already ordered: no extra memory.
steps.proof: You get 4 and 6.
steps.pitfall: Using this on unsorted input, where moving a pointer discards values that could still have matched.

problems.prompt: In [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], which pair sums to 10?
problems.answer: 4 and 6.

problems.prompt: The current sum is below the target. Which pointer moves, and which way?
problems.answer: The left one, rightwards, to increase the sum.

problems.prompt: Run the same 2 pointers on unsorted input. Which decision stops being safe?
problems.answer: Choosing which pointer to move, since a smaller value may lie in either direction.

steps.title: Remove in Place
steps.mastery: Compact an array using a slow and a fast index.
steps.practice: Remove every 2 from [2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 4] in place and report the new length.
steps.detail: The fast pointer reads every element; the slow one marks where the next keeper goes. Copy forward only when the value is kept, then the first slow elements are the answer. Nothing after the new length matters, which is what in place means here.
steps.proof: The first 3 elements are 1, 3, 4 and the new length is 3.
steps.pitfall: Deleting from the array while iterating over it, which skips elements.

problems.prompt: Remove every 2 from [2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 4]. What is the new length?
What does the slow pointer mark while the fast one reads all 6 elements?
problems.answer: The position the next kept element is written to.

problems.prompt: Do the elements after the new length of 3 matter?
problems.answer: No — only the first 3 are the result.

steps.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
steps.mastery: Interleave two ordered sequences with an index in each.
steps.practice: Merge [1, 4, 7] and [2, 3, 9] into 1 sorted array of 6 using an index per input.
steps.detail: Compare the fronts, take the smaller, advance that index. When one runs out, append the rest of the other — which is the part people forget, and it shows up as a lost tail rather than as an error.
steps.pitfall: Stopping when the first array is exhausted, which silently drops the remainder of the second.

problems.prompt: Merge [1, 4, 7] and [2, 3, 9]. What is the result?
What happens after 1 of the 2 inputs is exhausted?
problems.answer: The rest of the other is appended unchanged.

problems.prompt: What is the order of merging arrays of 3 and 3 elements, in terms of n and m?
problems.answer: O(n + m).

steps.title: Fast and Slow Pointers
steps.mastery: Use two pointers at different speeds to find a midpoint or a cycle.
steps.practice: Find the middle of a 7-element list with 1 pointer moving 1 step and another moving 2.
steps.detail: When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle — index 3 of 7. The same trick detects a cycle: if a fast pointer ever meets a slow one, the structure loops. Both need a careful check that fast and fast.next exist before advancing.
steps.proof: The slow pointer stops at index 3, the 4th element.
steps.pitfall: Advancing fast by 2 without checking fast.next, which raises on an even-length list.

problems.prompt: Where does the slow pointer end on a 7-element list?
problems.answer: At index 3, the middle element.

problems.prompt: What does it mean if a pointer moving 2 steps meets 1 moving 1 step?
problems.answer: The structure contains a cycle.

problems.prompt: What check is needed before advancing fast by 2?
problems.answer: That both fast and fast.next exist.

steps.title: Partition Around a Value
steps.mastery: Rearrange an array so one group precedes another.
steps.practice: Rearrange [3, 8, 1, 9, 4] so values under 5 come before the rest, using 2 pointers.
steps.detail: Walk from both ends: advance the left while its value belongs on the left, pull the right in while its value belongs on the right, then swap the 2 that are out of place. This is the partition step inside quicksort, and doing it by hand once makes that algorithm much less mysterious.
steps.proof: Every value under 5 sits before every value of 5 or more.
steps.pitfall: Swapping without advancing the pointers afterwards, which loops on the same pair.

problems.prompt: Partition [3, 8, 1, 9, 4] around 5. Which values end up first?
problems.answer: 3, 1 and 4, in some order, before 8 and 9.

problems.prompt: What 2 properties does a problem need for a 2-pointer solution?
problems.answer: Quicksort.

problems.prompt: You swap 2 out-of-place values and the loop repeats forever. What is missing?
problems.answer: The pointers are not advanced after the swap.

steps.title: Spot the Pattern
steps.mastery: Recognise when a problem admits a two-pointer solution.
steps.practice: Decide which of these 3 suit 2 pointers: pair sum on sorted data, longest substring, counting word frequencies.
steps.detail: Two pointers want a linear structure and a rule that lets you move one index without revisiting what it passed. Sorted data or a contiguous stretch usually provides that. A frequency count has no such ordering, so it wants a map instead.
steps.proof: The first 2 suit pointers; the frequency count wants a map.
steps.pitfall: Forcing 2 pointers onto unsorted data, which needs a sort first and may cost more than a map.

problems.prompt: Of these 3 — pair sum on sorted data, longest substring, word frequencies — which wants a map?
problems.answer: Word frequencies.

problems.prompt: What 2 properties does a 2-pointer solution need?
problems.answer: A linear structure, and a rule that makes moving a pointer safe.

problems.prompt: You force 2 pointers onto unsorted data. What is the extra cost?
problems.answer: An O(n log n) sort first, which may exceed the map solution.

steps.title: Track the Groups
steps.mastery: Represent group membership as a parent pointer per element.
steps.practice: Set up 5 elements as their own groups and print the parent array.
steps.detail: Each element starts as its own parent, so the array is [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] and there are 5 groups. A group is identified by the element at the top of its chain, which is the root, and nothing else about a group is stored.
steps.proof: The parent array holds each index pointing at itself, with 5 groups.
steps.pitfall: Storing a list of members per group, which makes a merge O(n) instead of O(1).

problems.prompt: What is the parent array for 5 elements in 5 separate groups?
problems.answer: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] — each its own parent.

problems.prompt: How is 1 group identified among 5?
problems.answer: By the root of its parent chain.

problems.prompt: Why not keep a member list per group of 5 elements?
problems.answer: A merge would then cost O(n) rather than a single pointer change.

steps.title: Find the Root
steps.mastery: Follow parent pointers to the top of a chain.
steps.practice: With parents [0, 0, 1, 3, 3], find the root of element 2 and count the hops.
steps.detail: Follow parent until an element is its own parent. Element 2 goes to 1, then to 0, which points at itself — 2 hops. Two elements are in the same group exactly when they share a root, which is the only comparison this structure makes.
steps.proof: The root of 2 is 0, after 2 hops.
steps.pitfall: Comparing parent pointers instead of roots, which calls 2 members of one group different.

problems.prompt: With parents [0, 0, 1, 3, 3], what is the root of element 2?
How many hops does the find of element 2 take?
When are elements 2 and 4 in the same group?
problems.answer: Only if they share a root — here they do not.

steps.title: Union Two Groups
steps.mastery: Merge two groups by pointing one root at the other.
steps.practice: Union elements 1 and 3 in a 5-element structure and print the parent array afterwards.
steps.detail: Find both roots; if they differ, point one at the other. That is a single assignment, which is why this structure is fast. If the roots match, the elements were already together and nothing happens.
steps.proof: One root now points at the other, and the group count falls from 5 to 4.
steps.pitfall: Pointing the element at the other element rather than root at root, which splits a group in 2.

problems.prompt: After unioning 1 and 3 in 5 singletons, how many groups remain?
What single assignment happens during a union of 2 groups?
problems.answer: One root's parent is set to the other root.

problems.prompt: You union 2 elements already in the same group. What changes?
problems.answer: Nothing.

steps.title: Union by Size
steps.mastery: Attach the smaller group under the larger to keep chains short.
steps.practice: Union a group of 4 with a group of 1 and say which root ends up on top.
steps.detail: Keep a size per root and always hang the smaller under the larger, so the deeper chain does not get deeper. Without it, unioning in a bad order builds a chain of n and find becomes O(n) — the same degeneration a search tree suffers.
steps.proof: The root of the 4-element group stays on top, and the depth does not grow.
steps.pitfall: Always attaching the first root under the second, which builds a chain on sorted input.

problems.prompt: Unioning a group of 4 with a group of 1, which root stays on top?
problems.answer: The root of the group of 4.

problems.prompt: What does a structure with no union by size degenerate to over 5 unions?
problems.answer: A chain, making find O(n).

problems.prompt: What extra value does each of the 2 roots store?
problems.answer: The size of its group.

steps.title: Compress the Path
steps.mastery: Flatten a chain during a find so later finds are shorter.
steps.practice: With parents [0, 0, 1, 2, 3], find the root of 4 and repoint every node on the path at it.
steps.detail: After the walk, set each visited node's parent to the root. The chain of 5 becomes depth 1, so the next find on any of them is a single hop. Combined with union by size this gives nearly constant time per operation.
steps.proof: Elements 1 to 4 all point directly at 0 afterwards.
steps.pitfall: Compressing only the queried node, which leaves the rest of the chain for the next caller.

problems.prompt: With parents [0, 0, 1, 2, 3], what do elements 1 to 4 point at after a compressed find of 4?
problems.answer: 0, directly.

problems.prompt: What does the next find on element 3 cost after compression?
problems.answer: 1 hop.

problems.prompt: Which 2 optimisations together give nearly constant time?
problems.answer: Union by size and path compression.

steps.title: Count the Components
steps.mastery: Maintain the number of separate groups as merges happen.
steps.practice: Start with 6 elements, apply the unions (0,1), (2,3) and (1,3), and give the group count.
steps.detail: Start the count at n and decrement on every union that actually merges 2 different roots. The third union here joins 2 existing groups, so 6 becomes 3. Counting roots at the end also works and costs a pass, which matters when the question is asked repeatedly.
steps.proof: The count ends at 3.
steps.pitfall: Decrementing on every union call, including ones where the roots already matched.

problems.prompt: 6 elements with unions (0,1), (2,3) and (1,3). How many groups remain?
When is the count of 6 decremented?
problems.answer: Only when a union joins 2 different roots.

problems.prompt: You union (0,1) twice. What is the count after, starting from 6?
problems.answer: 5 — the second call changes nothing.

steps.title: Detect a Cycle
steps.mastery: Use union-find to spot an edge that closes a loop.
steps.practice: Process the edges (0,1), (1,2) and (2,0) and identify which one closes a cycle.
steps.detail: For each edge, if the 2 ends already share a root the edge would close a cycle; otherwise union them. Here (2,0) is the cycle-closing edge. This is the test inside Kruskal's algorithm and the standard undirected cycle check.
steps.proof: The third edge is rejected as cycle-closing.
steps.pitfall: Unioning first and then checking, by which point every edge looks acceptable.

problems.prompt: Processing (0,1), (1,2), (2,0), which edge closes a cycle?
What is the test for an edge closing a cycle among 3 edges?
problems.answer: Its 2 ends already share a root.

problems.prompt: Which algorithm uses this test on 3 edges to build a minimum spanning tree?
problems.answer: Kruskal's.

steps.title: Know What It Cannot Do
steps.mastery: State the operation union-find does not support.
steps.practice: Say what happens if you need to undo the union of 2 groups, and name 1 workaround.
steps.detail: There is no split: the structure only merges, because a parent pointer records no history. If you need removals, process the merges in reverse — answer offline from the end backwards — or use a different structure. Knowing this stops you designing around an operation that does not exist.
steps.proof: You can state that splitting is unsupported and name the reverse-order workaround.
steps.pitfall: Planning a solution that removes an edge from a group, then discovering there is no split operation.

problems.prompt: Can union-find split 1 group back into 2?
problems.answer: No — it only merges.

problems.prompt: Name the standard workaround when 1 removal is needed.
problems.answer: Process the operations in reverse, so removals become merges.

problems.prompt: Why is there no split operation for 2 merged groups?
problems.answer: A parent pointer keeps no record of which merge created it.

steps.title: Simple if statement
steps.mastery: Recognize when a condition is true and execute a single statement.
steps.practice: Write an if statement that prints 'Hello' when variable x equals 10.
steps.detail: Assign x = 10 before the if. Use the equality operator == to compare x to 10. Place the print inside the indented block.
steps.proof: When x is set to 10, the program prints Hello; otherwise it prints nothing.
steps.pitfall: Using = instead of == in the condition.

steps.title: If‑else branch
steps.mastery: Choose between two actions based on a true or false condition.
steps.practice: Write an if‑else that prints 'Even' if number n is divisible by 2, otherwise prints 'Odd'.
steps.detail: Use n % 2 == 0 as the condition. End the if line with a colon, then indent the print statements. Ensure else is aligned with if.
steps.proof: For n = 4 the output is Even; for n = 5 the output is Odd.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the colon after the condition or mis‑indenting the else block.

steps.title: Multiple conditions with elif
steps.mastery: Select one of several mutually exclusive actions using elif.
steps.practice: Write an if‑elif‑else that prints 'Low' if score < 50, 'Medium' if score is between 50 and 79 inclusive, and 'High' if score ≥ 80.
steps.detail: Check the lowest range first (score < 50). Then use elif 50 <= score < 80 for the middle range, and else for the highest. Remember that Python evaluates conditions top‑down.
steps.proof: With score = 65 the program prints Medium; with score = 85 it prints High; with score = 30 it prints Low.
steps.pitfall: Using overlapping ranges or forgetting to include the equality sign on the boundary.

steps.title: Logical operators in conditions
steps.mastery: Combine simple comparisons with and, or, not to form complex conditions.
steps.practice: Write an if that prints 'Access granted' when user_age >= 18 and has_key == True.
steps.detail: Set variables user_age and has_key first. Use the and operator to require both sub‑conditions. Keep each comparison separate; no need for extra parentheses unless mixing with or.
steps.proof: If user_age = 20 and has_key = True the output is Access granted; if either is false nothing is printed.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'and' as '&' or forgetting parentheses when mixing and/or.

steps.title: Edge cases with inclusive ranges
steps.mastery: Write conditions that correctly handle boundary values without off‑by‑one errors.
steps.practice: Write an if that prints 'Valid' when 1 <= index < len(items) and prints 'Out of range' otherwise, assuming items = [10,20,30].
steps.detail: Create the list items. Use len(items) to get its length. The condition must be index >= 1 and index < len(items). Place the two prints in the if and else blocks.
steps.proof: With index = 0 the program prints Out of range; with index = 1 it prints Valid; with index = 3 it prints Out of range.
steps.pitfall: Using <= len(items) instead of < len(items), causing IndexError.

steps.title: Nested conditionals
steps.mastery: Embed one conditional inside another to handle dependent decisions.
steps.practice: Write code that asks for a number, checks if it is positive, and if so checks whether it is a multiple of 3, printing appropriate messages.
steps.detail: Use input() to read a number, convert to int. First if number > 0: print('Positive') then inside that block another if number % 3 == 0: print('Multiple of 3') else: print('Not a multiple of 3'). Add an else for the outer condition to print 'Not positive'.
steps.proof: For input 9 the program prints 'Positive' then 'Multiple of 3'; for -2 it prints only 'Not positive'.
steps.pitfall: Indenting the inner if at the same level as the outer if, breaking the nesting.

steps.title: Basic Try Except
steps.mastery: Wrap code in a try/except block to catch a specific exception.
steps.practice: Write a try/except block that catches FileNotFoundError when opening the file 'sample.txt'.
steps.detail: Place the code that may raise an error inside the try section. Follow it with except FileNotFoundError as e: and handle it, e.g., print a message. Do not put unrelated code after the try block.
steps.proof: The except clause runs and prints 'File not found' without crashing.
steps.pitfall: Catching a generic Exception instead of the specific FileNotFoundError.

steps.title: Multiple Exceptions
steps.mastery: Catch several specific exceptions in separate except clauses.
steps.practice: Write a try/except that catches ValueError when converting 'abc' to int and ZeroDivisionError when dividing 10 by 0.
steps.detail: List each except clause after the try, ordering from most specific to most general. Test each error path separately to verify the correct block runs.
steps.proof: Both except blocks print distinct messages and the program continues.
steps.pitfall: Using a single except: Exception: which swallows all errors and hides bugs.

steps.title: Else and Finally
steps.mastery: Employ else for code that runs only if no exception occurs and finally for cleanup.
steps.practice: Create a try/except/else/finally that opens 'data.txt', reads its content, prints it in else, and closes the file in finally.
steps.detail: Put the risky operation in try, handle errors in except, place the normal flow in else, and always put cleanup like file.close() in finally. This guarantees cleanup regardless of success or failure.
steps.proof: If the file exists, its contents are printed and the file is closed; if missing, only the except runs and finally still closes (or handles) the file.
steps.pitfall: Placing cleanup code inside else instead of finally, causing resources to stay open on error.

steps.title: Custom Exceptions
steps.mastery: Define and raise a user‑created exception class for domain‑specific errors.
steps.practice: Define class InvalidScoreError(Exception): pass and raise it when a variable score = -5 is less than 0.
steps.detail: Create a subclass of Exception with a descriptive name. Use raise InvalidScoreError('Score cannot be negative') where the condition is detected. This makes error handling clearer for callers.
steps.proof: The program aborts with InvalidScoreError and the traceback shows the custom name.
steps.pitfall: Raising a generic Exception instead of the custom class, losing semantic meaning.

steps.title: Input Validation
steps.mastery: Check user input before processing to prevent avoidable exceptions.
steps.practice: Write a function that asks for an integer via input(), validates it with int(), and reprompts up to 3 times before raising ValueError.
steps.detail: Use a loop that attempts int(user_input) inside try, catches ValueError, decrements attempts, and prompts again. After the loop, raise an error if no valid input was received.
steps.proof: The function returns a valid integer after correct entry or raises ValueError after three invalid attempts.
steps.pitfall: Relying on try/except alone without validating, leading to repeated crashes.

steps.title: Error Logging
steps.mastery: Record caught exceptions to a log file with traceback information.
steps.practice: Add a try/except around dividing 10 by int(user_input) that logs the exception to 'error.log' using the logging module.
steps.detail: Import logging, configure logging.basicConfig(filename='error.log', level=logging.ERROR). In except, call logging.exception('Division failed') to capture stack trace. This keeps a permanent record.
steps.proof: When non‑numeric input is given, 'error.log' contains the traceback and the program continues.
steps.pitfall: Printing errors to console only, losing persistent record for later analysis.

steps.title: Global Strategy
steps.mastery: Integrate consistent error handling across a program using a top‑level handler.
steps.practice: Wrap the main() function call in if __name__ == '__main__': with a try/except that catches any Exception, logs it, and exits with status 1.
steps.detail: Define a main() that contains program logic. At the script entry point, surround main() with try/except Exception as e: logging.exception('Unhandled error') and sys.exit(1). This ensures a uniform response to unexpected failures.
steps.proof: Any uncaught exception anywhere in the program triggers the top‑level except, logs the error, and the script exits with code 1.
steps.pitfall: Swallowing all exceptions silently without logging or proper exit code.

steps.title: Define a simple function
steps.mastery: Create a function that returns a fixed value without parameters.
steps.practice: Write a function named hello() that returns the string 'Hello'.
steps.detail: In Python, start with def hello(): then indent and write return 'Hello'. Ensure the return line is indented exactly one level. Save the file and run it to see the output.
steps.proof: Calling hello() returns 'Hello'.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the parentheses after the function name when calling it.

steps.title: Add parameters and return
steps.mastery: Define a function that accepts inputs and returns a computed result.
steps.practice: Write a function add(a, b) that returns a + b.
steps.detail: Use def add(a, b): then indent and write return a + b. Test with print(add(3,5)). The function should output 8.
steps.proof: Calling add(3, 5) returns 8.
steps.pitfall: Using = instead of == in a return expression, or forgetting to return the sum.

steps.title: Call a function and print
steps.mastery: Invoke a function and display its result using print.
steps.practice: Add a line print(hello()) after defining hello() from step 1.
steps.detail: After the function definition, write print(hello()). Run the script; the console should show Hello. Verify no errors appear.
steps.proof: The program prints Hello on the console.
steps.pitfall: Printing the function object instead of its return value, e.g., print(hello) without parentheses.

steps.title: Use function result in expression
steps.mastery: Combine a function's return value with other operations.
steps.practice: Write a function double(x) that returns 2 * x, then compute result = double(7) + 3 and print result.
steps.detail: Define def double(x): return 2 * x. Then write result = double(7) + 3; print(result). Run to see 17.
steps.proof: The program prints 17.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to assign the function call to a variable before adding, or mixing up order of operations.

steps.title: Multiple arguments and default
steps.mastery: Create a function with several parameters, some having default values.
steps.practice: Write a function power(base, exponent=2) that returns base ** exponent. Call power(5) and power(2,3) and print both results.
steps.detail: Use def power(base, exponent=2): return base ** exponent. Then print(power(5)) and print(power(2,3)). Verify outputs 25 and 8.
steps.proof: The program prints 25 and 8 on separate lines.
steps.pitfall: Omitting the default argument when defining, causing a TypeError when called with one argument.

steps.title: Build a small program with functions
steps.mastery: Design and use multiple functions to solve a problem without further guidance.
steps.practice: Write a program that defines (a) a function is_even(n) returning True if n % 2 == 0, (b) a function sum_evens(limit) that uses a loop to add all even numbers up to limit, and (c) prints sum_evens(20).
steps.detail: Define def is_even(n): return n % 2 == 0. Then def sum_evens(limit): total = 0; for i in range(1, limit+1): if is_even(i): total += i; return total. Finally, print(sum_evens(20)). Run to see 110.
steps.proof: The program prints 110 (the sum of even numbers 2 through 20).
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong comparison operator (e.g., = instead of ==) inside is_even, or forgetting to return a value.

steps.title: Read user input
steps.mastery: Use input() to capture a line of text from the user.
steps.practice: Prompt the user with "Enter your age: " and read the response into a variable called age_str using input().
steps.detail: Call input() with a prompt argument and assign the result to age_str. Remember input() always returns a string, even when the user types numbers. Test by typing a number and then printing age_str to see the captured value.
steps.proof: If the user types 27, age_str will contain the string "27".
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to include the prompt string inside input(), which results in a blank line before the user can type.

steps.title: Convert input to integer
steps.mastery: Transform a string input into an integer for numeric calculations.
steps.practice: Convert the variable age_str to an integer and store the result in a variable called age_int using int().
steps.detail: Wrap the string variable with int(): age_int = int(age_str). Verify the conversion by printing type(age_int). If an error occurs, ensure the original input contains only digits.
steps.proof: If age_str was "27", age_int will be the integer 27 and type(age_int) will be int.
steps.pitfall: Calling int() on a non‑numeric string, which raises a ValueError and stops the program.

steps.title: Print formatted output
steps.mastery: Display a message that includes variable values using f‑strings.
steps.practice: Calculate next_age = age_int + 1 and print an f‑string: "You will be {next_age} next year.".
steps.detail: Add 1 to age_int, assign to next_age, then use print(f"You will be {next_age} next year."). The f‑string inserts the integer automatically. Try different ages to see the output change.
steps.proof: If age_int was 29, the program prints: You will be 30 next year.
steps.pitfall: Using string concatenation without converting the integer, which causes a TypeError.

steps.title: Read from a file
steps.mastery: Open a text file, read its contents, and store them in a variable.
steps.practice: Create a file named data.txt containing the line 42 (no quotes). Write Python code that opens data.txt, reads the line, strips the newline, and stores it in a variable called file_number_str.
steps.detail: Use a with‑statement: with open('data.txt','r') as f: file_number_str = f.readline().strip(). The with‑statement ensures the file is closed automatically. Print file_number_str to confirm the value.
steps.proof: After the code runs, file_number_str will be the string "42".
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to close the file or using the wrong mode, which can leave the file open or return an empty string.

steps.title: Write output to a file
steps.mastery: Write computed results to a new text file using the write() method.
steps.practice: Create a string f"Current age: {age_int}, Next year: {next_age}" and write it to a file called result.txt in write mode.
steps.detail: Use with open('result.txt','w') as f: f.write(f"Current age: {age_int}, Next year: {next_age}"). The with‑statement handles closing. Open result.txt afterwards to verify its contents.
steps.proof: After execution, result.txt contains exactly: Current age: 29, Next year: 30 (assuming age_int was 29).
steps.pitfall: Opening result.txt in read mode ('r') instead of write mode ('w'), which prevents writing and may raise an error.

steps.title: Loop Concept Introduction
steps.mastery: Identify the three parts of a basic loop: initializer, condition, and update.
steps.practice: Write a for loop that prints the numbers 1 through 5.
steps.detail: Recall that a for loop needs a start value, an end condition, and a step. Use the range syntax to generate 1 to 5 inclusive, and place a print statement inside the loop body. Run the code and verify the five lines appear.
steps.proof: The program outputs each number on its own line: 1 2 3 4 5.
steps.pitfall: Omitting the update expression causes the loop to run forever.

steps.title: Counting with While
steps.mastery: Construct a while loop that repeats until a numeric condition becomes false.
steps.practice: Write a while loop that starts with n = 3, prints n, then decrements n until it reaches 0.
steps.detail: Initialize n before the loop, then use while n > 0: print n and subtract 1 inside the body. The condition is checked before each iteration, so the loop stops when n becomes 0. Verify the three numbers appear in descending order.
steps.proof: The output is three lines: 3 2 1.
steps.pitfall: Using > instead of >= in the condition skips the last value.

steps.title: Iterating Over a List
