steps.practice: Compare your paper scores at the start and end of 3 weeks, and say which topics moved.
steps.detail: A completed timetable is not the goal; a higher score is. Sit a paper in week 1 and another in week 3 under the same conditions, then compare by topic. A topic that got 6 hours and did not move needs a different method rather than more time, which is the most useful thing this comparison tells you.
steps.proof: Two comparable paper scores with a per-topic difference.
steps.pitfall: Judging the 3 weeks by how much of the timetable was completed.

problems.prompt: A topic got 6 hours across 3 weeks and its score did not move. More time or a different method?
problems.answer: A different method — 6 hours of the same approach has already been tested.

problems.prompt: Why sit the week-1 and week-3 papers under the same conditions?
problems.answer: Otherwise the difference measures the conditions rather than the revision.

problems.prompt: Which is the better measure of 3 weeks: 34 of 36 slots ticked, or 12 marks gained per paper?
problems.answer: The marks — the slots measure activity, not progress.

steps.title: Write the Finish Line
steps.mastery: Define what finishing looks like before starting a self-taught subject.
steps.practice: Write 1 sentence naming what you will be able to do at the end, with 2 things that will prove it.
steps.detail: With no course there is no syllabus and no exam, so the finish line has to be written or the project drifts. "Read a 200-line Python script and explain what it does" is a finish line; "learn Python" is not. The 2 proofs are what you will actually produce, and they double as the test.
steps.proof: 1 sentence and 2 named proofs you could show somebody.
steps.pitfall: Starting with "learn X", which has no end and therefore no progress.

problems.prompt: Which is a finish line: (a) learn Spanish, (b) hold a 10-minute conversation about your job in Spanish?
problems.answer: (b). It names something you can do and check.

problems.prompt: What do the 2 proofs also serve as?
problems.answer: The test of whether the subject is finished.

problems.prompt: Why does "learn Python" produce drift?
problems.answer: It has no end, so no session can be measured against it.

steps.title: Build the Syllabus
steps.mastery: Sequence a subject yourself, in dependency order.
steps.practice: Break your subject into 8 topics and draw 6 arrows showing which topic each one needs first.
steps.detail: Take the contents pages of 2 or 3 books and look for the order they agree on — that agreement is most of a syllabus. Then draw the dependencies, because the order you learn in matters more than the list. Where 2 books disagree on order, either is usually fine.
steps.proof: 8 topics with 6 dependency arrows, built from the agreement between 2 sources.
steps.pitfall: Inventing an order from scratch, when 3 contents pages already encode one.

problems.prompt: Where does the order for 8 topics come from most cheaply?
problems.answer: The agreement between the contents pages of 2 or 3 books.

problems.prompt: Two books disagree on whether topic 4 comes before topic 5. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick either — where sources disagree, the order usually does not matter much.

problems.prompt: Why are the 6 arrows more important than the list of 8?
problems.answer: The learning order decides whether each topic is met with what it depends on.

steps.title: Set Your Own Deadline
steps.mastery: Impose a date that makes a self-taught project finite.
steps.practice: Set a date 10 weeks out, divide your 8 topics across it, and write the 2 checkpoint dates.
steps.detail: Nobody else will supply the deadline, and without one the project expands until it is abandoned. Ten weeks, 8 topics, with checkpoints at weeks 4 and 8 where you produce something. Tell somebody the date, because a deadline nobody knows about is a wish.
steps.proof: A finish date, 8 topics allocated, and 2 checkpoint dates somebody else knows.
steps.pitfall: Setting a date privately and moving it twice, which is the same as having none.

problems.prompt: 10 weeks and 8 topics. Roughly how long does each topic get?
problems.answer: About 9 days.

problems.prompt: Why tell somebody else the 10-week finish date?
problems.answer: A private deadline gets moved, and a moved deadline is no deadline.

problems.prompt: What happens at the week-4 and week-8 checkpoints?
problems.answer: You produce something that shows where the project actually is.

steps.title: Find the Problem Set
steps.mastery: Locate answered exercises for a subject nobody is setting you work in.
steps.practice: Find 2 sources of answered problems for your subject and work 5 of them today.
steps.detail: Self-teaching fails most often here: reading is easy to arrange and problems are not, so people read 6 books and cannot do anything. Look for textbooks with answers, problem collections, online judges or past papers. Without answers you cannot mark yourself, and unmarked practice entrenches errors.
steps.proof: 2 named sources with answers, and 5 problems worked and marked today.
steps.pitfall: Settling for a source with no answers because it is the one you found.

problems.prompt: Why is a source of 200 problems with no answers close to useless for self-teaching?
problems.answer: You cannot mark yourself, so errors get entrenched rather than caught.

problems.prompt: Name 2 kinds of source that supply answered problems.
problems.answer: Textbooks with answer sections, and past papers with mark schemes.

problems.prompt: You have read 6 books and worked 0 problems. What is the diagnosis?
problems.answer: Reading has replaced practice, which is the usual way self-teaching fails.

steps.title: Schedule It Like a Course
steps.mastery: Put self-taught work in fixed slots rather than in spare time.
steps.practice: Fix 3 weekly slots of 60 minutes for the subject and defend them for 2 weeks.
steps.detail: Spare time is the time that disappears first, so a subject living there is a subject that stops. Three fixed hours a week beats a nominal 10 that happen twice. Record kept or missed, because 2 weeks of that record tells you whether the slots are real.
steps.proof: A 2-week record of the 3 weekly slots, marked kept or missed.
steps.pitfall: Planning 10 hours a week of spare time, which produces 2 and a sense of failure.

problems.prompt: Which is better: 3 fixed hours a week or a nominal 10 in spare time?
problems.answer: The 3 fixed hours — spare time is what disappears first.

problems.prompt: You keep 3 of 6 slots over 2 weeks. What does the record suggest?
problems.answer: The slots are not realistically free and need moving.

problems.prompt: Why record slots kept and missed rather than the 10 hours studied?
problems.answer: It tests whether the schedule itself is real.

steps.title: Test Yourself on Schedule
steps.mastery: Create the tests a course would have set you.
steps.practice: Write a 10-question test for your first 2 topics, sit it cold a week later, and mark it.
steps.detail: Without tests, self-teaching runs on the feeling of understanding, which is exactly the thing that is unreliable. Write the test as you finish the topic, while you know what was hard, then leave it a week so sitting it is a real test. Mark it strictly against what you wrote.
steps.proof: A 10-question test, sat a week later, with a marked score.
steps.pitfall: Writing the test and sitting it the same afternoon, which measures the afternoon.

problems.prompt: When do you write the 10-question test, and when do you sit it?
problems.answer: Write it as the topic finishes; sit it about a week later.

problems.prompt: Why does sitting your own 10-question test the same afternoon measure very little?
problems.answer: The material is still in short-term memory, so it tests the afternoon.

problems.prompt: With 0 tests, what does self-teaching run on?
problems.answer: The feeling of understanding, which is the unreliable part.

steps.title: Get One Outside Reader
steps.mastery: Have somebody else check work nobody is marking.
steps.practice: Send 1 piece of your work to somebody who knows the subject and ask for 2 specific criticisms.
steps.detail: Self-teaching has no marker, and the errors you cannot see are exactly the ones you need found. Ask for 2 criticisms rather than an opinion, because "looks good" costs somebody nothing and tells you nothing. A forum, a colleague or a tutor for an hour all work.
steps.proof: 2 specific criticisms received, and 1 line on what each changes.
steps.pitfall: Asking whether the work is good, which invites encouragement rather than correction.

problems.prompt: Ask for an opinion or for 2 specific criticisms?
problems.answer: 2 specific criticisms — an opinion invites encouragement rather than correction.

problems.prompt: Why does a self-taught subject with 0 markers particularly need an outside reader?
problems.answer: There is no marker, so the errors you cannot see stay unfound.

problems.prompt: Name 2 places an outside reader can come from.
problems.answer: A subject forum, or a colleague or tutor for an hour.

steps.title: Keep a Work Log
steps.mastery: Record what each session produced so progress is visible without grades.
steps.practice: Log 6 sessions with 1 line each on what was produced, and read the 6 back.
steps.detail: A course supplies marks, deadlines and the sense of moving; a log is the substitute. One line per session naming the output — problems solved, pages read, a script that runs — and nothing about how it felt. Reading 6 back is what tells you whether the project is moving or circling.
steps.proof: 6 logged lines, each naming an output, read back in one go.
steps.pitfall: Logging hours and moods, which produces a diary rather than a record of progress.

problems.prompt: Which log line is usable: (a) "2 hours, felt slow", (b) "solved 8 of 10 exercises on gradients"?
problems.answer: (b). It names output.

problems.prompt: What does reading 6 lines back in one go tell you?
problems.answer: Whether the project is moving or circling the same ground.

problems.prompt: In a self-taught subject, what do the 6 logged lines replace?
problems.answer: The marks and deadlines a course would have supplied.

steps.title: Finish and Prove It
steps.mastery: Deliver the proof you named at the start and judge yourself against it.
steps.practice: Produce the 2 proofs from your finish line and have 1 of them checked by somebody else.
steps.detail: Finishing is a decision, and without proofs the subject stays 80 per cent done forever. Produce both, compare them against the sentence you wrote at the start, and be strict: if a proof came out thinner than intended, name what is missing rather than adjusting the finish line to fit.
steps.proof: Both proofs produced, 1 externally checked, and a verdict against the original sentence.
steps.pitfall: Moving the finish line to match what you managed, which makes the whole exercise unfalsifiable.

problems.prompt: A proof comes out thinner than the finish line asked for. Adjust the line or name the gap?
problems.answer: Name the gap — adjusting the line makes the project unfalsifiable.

problems.prompt: Why have 1 of the 2 proofs checked externally?
problems.answer: Self-assessment at the finish is the least reliable point to rely on it.

problems.prompt: What keeps a self-taught subject at 80 per cent done forever?
problems.answer: Having no named proofs, so finishing is never a decision that can be made.

steps.title: Choose the Next Subject
steps.mastery: Use what one self-taught project revealed to pick and plan the next.
steps.practice: Write 3 lines on what went wrong in this project and 1 change you will make to the next plan.
steps.detail: The second self-taught subject should be cheaper than the first, and it only is if the failures are recorded: the slots that were not real, the reading that replaced problems, the finish line that was too vague. One change, not 6, carried into the next plan and checked at its first checkpoint.
steps.proof: 3 recorded failures and 1 specific change written into the next project's plan.
steps.pitfall: Starting the next subject the same way and finding out the same things again.

problems.prompt: Why 1 change carried forward rather than 6?
problems.answer: One gets applied and checked; 6 gets forgotten by week 2.

problems.prompt: Name 2 failures worth recording from a first self-taught project.
problems.answer: Slots that were never really free, and reading that replaced problem practice.

problems.prompt: When is the 1 carried change checked?
problems.answer: At the next project's first checkpoint, in about week 4.

steps.title: Start From the Question
steps.mastery: Choose material by the gap it fills rather than by what is available.
steps.practice: Write the 1 question you need answered, then name 2 sources likely to answer it and 1 that will not.
steps.detail: Searching before the question is stated is how 3 hours go on a reading list. State the gap in a sentence — "why does the sign flip when the inequality is multiplied by a negative" — and the right kind of source becomes obvious: a worked-examples book, not a lecture series.
steps.proof: 1 written question, 2 candidate sources, and a reason the third was rejected.
steps.pitfall: Collecting 6 promising sources before knowing which question they are for.

problems.prompt: Your question is "why does the inequality sign flip on multiplying by -2". Which is the better source: a 40-minute lecture or a worked-examples page?
problems.answer: The worked-examples page — the question is narrow and specific.

problems.prompt: You have 6 sources and no written question. What is the next action?
problems.answer: Write the question, then discard the sources that do not answer it.

problems.prompt: Why does stating the gap in 1 sentence narrow the search?
problems.answer: The form of the answer implies the kind of source that carries it.

steps.title: Past Papers First
steps.mastery: Use past papers to see what is actually asked before reading around.
steps.practice: Take 3 past papers and tally how many marks each topic carried across them.
steps.detail: A syllabus lists topics; past papers show weights. Tallying 3 papers by topic usually shows 2 or 3 topics carrying a third of the marks and several worth 4 marks in 3 years. That tally decides where the reading goes, and it takes about 20 minutes to build.
steps.proof: A tally of marks per topic across 3 papers.
steps.pitfall: Working the papers for practice before reading them for pattern, which loses the survey.

problems.prompt: Across 3 papers, topic A carries 34 marks and topic B carries 6. Where does the reading go?
problems.answer: Mostly to topic A, which is nearly 6 times the weight.

problems.prompt: What does a syllabus not tell you that 3 past papers do?
problems.answer: How the marks are actually distributed across the topics.

problems.prompt: Why read the 3 papers for pattern before working them for practice?
problems.answer: Once they are worked they are no longer a clean survey of what gets asked.

steps.title: Judge a Textbook Fast
steps.mastery: Decide in 10 minutes whether a book answers your question.
steps.practice: Open 2 textbooks at the same topic and compare how each treats 1 worked example, in 10 minutes.
steps.detail: Check 3 things: does it work examples in full, does it state results you can check, and is the exercise set answered. A book that explains beautifully with no answered exercises is a bad study book however good the prose. Compare at the topic you are stuck on, not at chapter 1.
steps.proof: A 1-line verdict on each book, naming the deciding difference.
steps.pitfall: Judging by the introduction, which is the part written to be persuasive.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 things this step checks in a textbook.
problems.answer: Whether examples are worked in full, whether results are checkable, and whether exercises have answers.

problems.prompt: Book A explains beautifully with no answers; book B is terse with 200 answered exercises. Which to study from?
problems.answer: B — you cannot mark your work from A.

problems.prompt: Why compare the 2 books at the topic you are stuck on rather than at chapter 1?
problems.answer: Chapter 1 is written to persuade; the hard topic shows how the book actually teaches.

steps.title: Check Who Wrote It
steps.mastery: Establish a source's authority before trusting its content.
steps.practice: Take 2 online explanations of 1 topic and find who wrote each, then say which you would trust and why.
steps.detail: Look for an author, an institution, a date and something checkable — a reference, a derivation, a worked answer. A confident page with no author and no working is not a source, whatever the ranking said. Where you cannot establish authority, verify the claim against a second source before using it.
steps.proof: For each of the 2: an author or institution, a date, and your verdict.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a page because it is clearly written, which is uncorrelated with being right.

problems.prompt: A page has no author, no date and 3 confident claims. Usable or not?
problems.answer: Not on its own — verify each claim against a second source first.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things that make an explanation checkable rather than just confident.
problems.answer: A derivation you can follow and a worked answer you can verify.

problems.prompt: Why is clarity a poor proxy for correctness in 1 sentence?
problems.answer: A wrong explanation can be written just as clearly as a right one.

steps.title: Two Sources on a Hard Point
steps.mastery: Read 2 accounts of the same difficulty and use the difference.
steps.practice: Read 2 explanations of 1 topic you find hard and write the 1 sentence where they differ most.
steps.detail: When 1 explanation does not land, a second rarely repeats it — different books cut the idea in different places, and the join between the 2 cuts is often where your difficulty was. Where they conflict outright, that is worth resolving rather than averaging, and a third source settles it.
steps.proof: 1 sentence naming the biggest difference between the 2 accounts.
steps.pitfall: Rereading the same explanation 4 times on the theory that it will eventually land.

problems.prompt: Two sources conflict on a definition. Average them or find a 3rd?
problems.answer: Find a 3rd — a conflict is a fact to resolve, not to split.

problems.prompt: Why does a 2nd explanation help where rereading the 1st 4 times does not?
problems.answer: It cuts the idea in a different place, often exactly where the difficulty was.

problems.prompt: You read 2 accounts and they agree completely. What have you gained?
problems.answer: Confidence in the account, though not the alternative angle the step was after.

steps.title: Keep a Source List
steps.mastery: Record where each answer came from so it can be found again.
steps.practice: Start a list holding 6 sources with 1 line each on what it answered well.
steps.detail: Note what a source was good for rather than what it was about — "clear on why the discriminant decides the root count" is findable later; "algebra book" is not. Keep it to 1 file with the date you used each one, and cross out sources that disappointed you rather than deleting them.
steps.proof: 6 entries, each naming what that source answered.
steps.pitfall: Keeping 30 bookmarks with no note of what any of them was for.

problems.prompt: Which entry is useful in 6 months: (a) "stats textbook", (b) "clear on why n-1 appears in the sample variance"?
problems.answer: (b). It says what the source answered.

problems.prompt: Why cross out a disappointing source rather than delete it from a list of 6?
problems.answer: So you do not return to it a 2nd time having forgotten.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 fields every entry carries?
problems.answer: What it answered well, and the date you used it.

steps.title: Stop Collecting, Start Working
steps.mastery: Cap the search and begin with what you have.
steps.practice: Give a search 15 minutes, then stop and work the best source you found for 45 minutes.
steps.detail: Collecting feels like progress and is almost free of difficulty, which is why it expands. A 15-minute cap and a named next action ends it. If the source turns out wrong 20 minutes in, that is a result — go back and search again with a sharper question, not a longer list.
steps.proof: A 15-minute search, then 45 minutes of work in the source it chose.
steps.pitfall: Continuing to search because none of the 8 sources is perfect, which is how a week goes.

problems.prompt: You have spent 50 minutes finding sources and 0 working. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stop searching and work the best source you have for 45 minutes.

problems.prompt: The chosen source proves wrong 20 minutes in. Search longer next time or sharpen the question?
problems.answer: Sharpen the question — the list was not the problem.

problems.prompt: Why does collecting 8 sources expand to fill the time available?
problems.answer: It resembles progress and involves none of the difficulty of the actual work.

steps.title: Match Source to Stage
steps.mastery: Pick the kind of source that suits how far into a topic you are.
steps.practice: For 1 topic, name the source you would use at first contact, at practice stage, and 3 days before an exam.
steps.detail: First contact wants a clear linear explanation; practice wants a bank of answered problems; the last week wants past papers and your own 1-page summaries. Using the wrong one is why revision sometimes feels like starting again — a textbook chapter 3 days out is a source for a different stage.
steps.proof: 3 named sources, 1 per stage, with a reason each.
steps.pitfall: Opening a fresh textbook 3 days before an exam, which is first-contact material at the wrong time.

problems.prompt: Which source suits the 3 days before an exam: a new textbook chapter or 4 past papers?
problems.answer: The past papers — new material at that stage is first-contact work.

problems.prompt: What kind of source suits the practice stage, once 1 pass through the topic is done?
problems.answer: A bank of problems with answers you can mark yourself against.

problems.prompt: Why does opening a new textbook 3 days out make revision feel like starting again?
problems.answer: First-contact material re-teaches ground you have already covered instead of testing it.

steps.title: First Review Next Day
steps.mastery: Put the first review of new material inside 24 hours of meeting it.
steps.practice: Test 15 cards from today's material again tomorrow, before any of it is reread.
steps.detail: The steepest part of forgetting happens in the first day, so the first review is the one that pays most and the one most people skip. Put it in the calendar as you finish the material, not later — a review that has to be remembered is a review that does not happen.
steps.proof: Tomorrow's session opens with today's 15 cards and a score for them.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the first review 3 days because the material still feels fresh on day 1.

problems.prompt: You meet 20 new terms on Monday. When is the first review, and what does it consist of?
problems.answer: Tuesday, testing all 20 before any rereading.

problems.prompt: Which schedule loses more: (a) first review on day 1, (b) first review on day 4?
problems.answer: (b). Most forgetting happens inside the first day, so the day-4 review re-learns rather than reviews.

problems.prompt: Why schedule the day-1 review while finishing the material rather than the next morning?
problems.answer: A review that depends on remembering to do it is one that gets skipped.

steps.title: Double the Gap
steps.mastery: Grow the interval after each success so reviews cost less over time.
steps.practice: Set the next 4 review dates for a card first learned on day 1, doubling from a 2-day gap.
steps.detail: Start at 2 days and double while the card keeps coming back right: day 3, day 7, day 15, day 31. The gaps grow because a card recalled after a week is stronger than one recalled after a day, so it does not need asking again soon. Write the next date on the card rather than keeping the schedule in your head.
steps.proof: The card carries 4 dates — days 3, 7, 15 and 31 — and each was set when the previous review passed.
steps.pitfall: Doubling the gap after a review you only half-passed, which loses the card entirely.

problems.prompt: A card is learned on day 1 and reviewed at a 2-day gap that doubles. Give the next 3 review days.
problems.answer: Day 3, day 7, then day 15.

problems.prompt: Your day-7 review of a card is a miss. What happens to the gap?
problems.answer: It resets to 2 days rather than doubling to 15.

problems.prompt: Why does a card recalled after 14 days need asking less often than one recalled after 1 day?
problems.answer: Recall after a long gap is evidence the memory is durable, so the next gap can be longer still.

steps.title: Reset on a Miss
steps.mastery: Send a failed card back to a short interval instead of nudging it.
steps.practice: Take 5 cards missed at a 15-day gap and reschedule each to 2 days rather than 10.
steps.detail: A miss means the interval overtook the memory, and the fix is to go back near the start rather than to trim a few days off. It feels wasteful and is not: a card reset to 2 days and passed 3 times will outlast one that has been limping at 10-day gaps for a month.
steps.proof: All 5 missed cards sit at a 2-day gap, and none kept a gap longer than the one it failed at.
steps.pitfall: Dropping a missed card from 15 days to 10 so the deck stays small, which keeps failing it.

problems.prompt: A card fails at a 15-day gap. Reset it to 2 days or trim it to 10?
problems.answer: Reset it to 2 days — the interval already outran the memory.

problems.prompt: You reset 5 cards to 2 days. How many extra reviews does that add this week, and is it worth it?
problems.answer: About 10, and yes — 3 short passes make the card durable where a trimmed gap keeps failing.

problems.prompt: State the signal that a 15-day interval was set too long.
problems.answer: A miss at that interval, which is the deck telling you the gap overtook the memory.

steps.title: One Deck, Daily Slice
steps.mastery: Work a single dated deck so each day's review is only what is due.
steps.practice: Sort 60 cards by their next date and work only the 9 due today.
steps.detail: Dating every card turns a deck you cannot face into a daily slice you can. Sort once, then each session take the front of the pile until the dates run ahead of today and stop, even if you have time left — the cards behind are not due and working them early collapses the schedule.
steps.proof: Today's session held exactly the 9 due cards, and the rest of the 60 were untouched.
steps.pitfall: Carrying on into tomorrow's cards because the session felt short, which bunches the deck up again.

problems.prompt: Of 60 dated cards, 9 are due today and 14 tomorrow. How many do you work today?
problems.answer: 9. Tomorrow's 14 stay where they are.

problems.prompt: You finish today's 9 cards with 10 minutes spare. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stop. Working ahead pulls tomorrow's cards forward and collapses the spacing.

problems.prompt: Why does dating each card make a 300-card deck workable?
problems.answer: Because a session only ever holds the few dozen that are due, not the whole deck.

steps.title: Spacing Across Subjects
steps.mastery: Fit several subjects' due cards into one daily block without dropping any.
steps.practice: Plan a 30-minute block covering 3 subjects with 8, 6 and 5 cards due.
steps.detail: Add the due cards up first, then divide the block — 19 cards in 30 minutes is about 90 seconds each, which is enough for a spoken answer and a mark. If the total will not fit, cut the subject with the shortest gaps rather than skipping a whole subject, because a skipped day resets every card in it.
steps.proof: All 19 due cards were worked inside the 30 minutes, across all 3 subjects.
steps.pitfall: Giving the first subject 25 of the 30 minutes and abandoning the third, which resets its whole schedule.

problems.prompt: 3 subjects have 8, 6 and 5 cards due in a 30-minute block. How long per card?
problems.answer: About 95 seconds — 19 cards into 30 minutes.

problems.prompt: 22 cards are due and you have 15 minutes. Which do you cut?
problems.answer: Some of the shortest-gap cards, which come round again soonest — not a whole subject.

problems.prompt: What happens to a subject's schedule when its day is skipped entirely?
problems.answer: Every card in it overruns its interval, so the next session is re-learning rather than review.

steps.title: Keep the Schedule Honest
steps.mastery: Audit a spacing schedule against what you actually did, weekly.
steps.practice: Count the cards that came due in the last 7 days and how many you actually worked.
steps.detail: Write both numbers down: due and done. A ratio under about 0.8 means the schedule is fiction and the deck is silently growing a backlog, which ends with a session nobody can face. The fix is fewer new cards this week, not a longer session next week.
steps.proof: You can state last week's due count, done count and the ratio between them.
steps.pitfall: Adding 20 new cards in a week where only half the due ones got worked.

problems.prompt: 70 cards came due last week and you worked 42. Give the ratio and what it means.
problems.answer: 0.6 — a backlog is building and the schedule is not being kept.

problems.prompt: Your done-to-due ratio is 0.5. Do you lengthen the sessions or add fewer new cards?
problems.answer: Add fewer new cards. The intake is what created the backlog.

problems.prompt: Why record both the due count and the done count rather than only a score of 8 out of 10?
problems.answer: A high score on half the due cards hides a backlog that a score alone cannot show.

steps.title: One Page Per Topic
steps.mastery: Compress a topic onto a single page with nothing left off that matters.
steps.practice: Compress 12 pages of notes onto 1 side, keeping every result and dropping every example.
steps.detail: The constraint does the teaching: with 1 side you have to decide what the topic is actually made of. Keep definitions, results and the 1 or 2 worked patterns; drop prose, repeated examples and anything you could rebuild. If it will not fit, the topic is 2 topics.
steps.proof: 1 side that lets you answer questions on the topic without the original 12 pages.
steps.pitfall: Shrinking the handwriting to fit 12 pages onto 1, which compresses nothing.

problems.prompt: Which goes on the 1 page: (a) 3 worked examples of the same type, (b) the result they all illustrate?
problems.answer: (b). One pattern is kept; the repeats are dropped.

problems.prompt: Your 12 pages will not fit on 1 side. What is the likely cause?
problems.answer: The material is 2 topics and wants splitting into 2 pages.

problems.prompt: Why is writing smaller not a compression of 12 pages?
problems.answer: Nothing was decided about what matters — the same content is still there.

steps.title: Draw What Connects
steps.mastery: Show the relationships in a topic as a diagram rather than a list.
steps.practice: Draw 8 concepts from 1 topic as boxes and label every arrow between them with a verb.
steps.detail: Labelling the arrows is the part that does the work: "causes", "is a case of", "is measured by" are different relationships, and an unlabelled arrow hides which you meant. Eight boxes is enough for a topic and few enough to lay out. Arrows you cannot label are relationships you have not understood.
steps.proof: A diagram of 8 boxes where every arrow carries a verb.
steps.pitfall: Drawing 20 boxes joined by bare lines, which records the vocabulary and none of the structure.

problems.prompt: Label the arrow between "friction" and "heat" with a verb.
problems.answer: Friction generates heat.

problems.prompt: Why must each of the 8 diagram's arrows carry a verb?
problems.answer: Different relationships look identical as bare lines, so the structure is lost.

problems.prompt: You cannot label 2 of your 9 arrows. What have you found?
problems.answer: Two relationships you have not understood, which are the next thing to study.

steps.title: Hierarchy, Not a List
steps.mastery: Arrange a topic's content by what contains what.
steps.practice: Rearrange 15 flat bullet points into 3 groups with 2 levels of indentation.
steps.detail: A flat list of 15 says everything is equally important, which is never true. Find the 3 or 4 organising ideas, then put the rest underneath where they belong. The grouping is a claim about the subject and can be wrong, which is exactly why it is worth making.
steps.proof: 15 points under 3 headings, and you can defend each placement.
steps.pitfall: Grouping by where things appeared in the book rather than by what they belong to.

problems.prompt: What does a flat list of 15 equal bullets claim about the material?
problems.answer: That all 15 matter equally, which is almost never true.

problems.prompt: Should 15 points be grouped by chapter order or by what contains what?
problems.answer: By what contains what — chapter order is the book's structure, not the subject's.

problems.prompt: Why is a grouping of 15 points worth making even when it might be wrong?
problems.answer: It is a claim about the subject, so being wrong is something you can find and fix.

steps.title: Summarise From Memory
steps.mastery: Produce the one-page summary without the notes open.
steps.practice: Rebuild your 1-page summary from blank paper, then compare it against the original and mark 3 differences.
steps.detail: Copying a summary teaches nothing; producing one is the whole exercise. Write it cold, then lay it beside the original. The differences fall into 2 kinds — things you forgot, and things you chose to leave off this time — and only the first kind is a gap.
steps.proof: A rebuilt page with the differences marked and sorted into forgotten and dropped.
steps.pitfall: Treating every difference as a memory failure, when some are better editing.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 kinds of difference between a remembered summary and the original.
problems.answer: Things forgotten, and things deliberately dropped as unnecessary.

problems.prompt: Your rebuilt page is 1 third shorter and still answers every question. What does that mean?
problems.answer: The original carried a third more than the topic needed.

problems.prompt: Why produce the summary cold rather than copying the 1-page original?
problems.answer: Copying tests handwriting; producing it tests the topic.

steps.title: Link Two Topics
steps.mastery: Connect 2 separate summaries at the point they actually meet.
steps.practice: Put 2 one-page summaries side by side and write 3 links between them, each naming the shared idea.
steps.detail: Topics are taught separately and examined together, so the joins are worth making explicitly. A link needs the shared idea named — "both are conservation arguments" — rather than a line drawn between 2 pages. Write each link on both pages so either one leads to the other.
steps.proof: 3 named links, written on both summaries.
steps.pitfall: Linking 2 topics because they appeared in the same chapter, which is not a shared idea.

problems.prompt: Which is a real link: (a) both topics were in chapter 4, (b) both are conservation arguments?
problems.answer: (b). The first is a fact about the book.

problems.prompt: Why write each of the 3 links on both pages?
problems.answer: So either page leads to the other, whichever one you open.

problems.prompt: Name 1 shared idea between momentum and money supply worth writing as a link.
problems.answer: Both are quantities conserved in a closed system unless something enters or leaves.

steps.title: Compress the Compression
steps.mastery: Reduce a one-page summary to a card without losing what it recovers.
steps.practice: Reduce 1 page of summary to 10 lines on a card, and check the card still recovers the page.
steps.detail: The second compression is where the organising ideas separate from the details: 10 lines can only hold structure, so anything that survives is load-bearing. Test by writing the page back from the card. What is missing from the rebuild goes back on the card, replacing something that was not needed.
steps.proof: A 10-line card that lets you rebuild the page, tested once.
steps.pitfall: Writing 10 lines of headings, which recovers the topics and none of the content.

problems.prompt: Which card is better: 10 headings, or 6 headings and 4 key results?
problems.answer: The second — headings alone recover the topics but not the content.

problems.prompt: You rebuild the page from the card and 2 results are missing. What changes on the card?
problems.answer: The 2 results go on, replacing lines that were not needed.

problems.prompt: Why does a 10-line limit reveal which ideas are load-bearing?
problems.answer: Only structure fits, so anything surviving the cut is doing real work.

steps.title: Summarise a Whole Course
steps.mastery: Fit a term's material onto one sheet that shows how the parts relate.
steps.practice: Put 8 topic cards onto 1 A3 sheet, with 6 arrows showing which topic a later one depends on.
steps.detail: This is the map you revise from, and its value is the arrows rather than the boxes: seeing that topic 7 needs topic 3 tells you the order to revise in and which failures will cascade. Build it from the cards you already have, and leave room to add arrows as you notice them.
steps.proof: 1 sheet with 8 topics and 6 dependency arrows you can each justify.
steps.pitfall: Laying the 8 topics out in the order they were taught, which hides the dependencies.

problems.prompt: Topic 7 depends on topic 3. What does that tell you about the revision order?
problems.answer: Topic 3 gets revised before 7, and failing 3 undermines both.

problems.prompt: Why are the 6 arrows more useful than the 8 boxes?
problems.answer: The boxes list the course; the arrows say what order it has to be learned in.

problems.prompt: What is wrong with laying 8 topics out in teaching order?
problems.answer: Teaching order is not dependency order, so the cascades stay hidden.

steps.title: Sort Given From Derived
steps.mastery: Separate what a subject asserts from what follows from it.
steps.practice: Split 10 facts from 1 topic into 2 columns: given by definition, and derivable from the others.
steps.detail: Definitions have to be memorised; consequences do not, because they can be rebuilt. Sorting them tells you how much of a topic is genuinely arbitrary — usually far less than it feels. For each derived fact write the 1 line of reasoning that recovers it from the givens.
steps.proof: The derived column has a 1-line derivation beside each entry, and the given column has none.
steps.pitfall: Filing something as given because you cannot derive it yet, which hides the reasoning you were about to learn.

problems.prompt: Is "a circle's area is pi r squared" given or derived, and from what?
problems.answer: Derived — it follows from the definition of pi and the limit of inscribed polygons.

problems.prompt: Of 10 facts you file 8 as given. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: Most are consequences you cannot yet derive, so the derivations are the work.

problems.prompt: Why does sorting 10 facts this way reduce what has to be memorised?
problems.answer: Anything derivable can be rebuilt from the few genuine definitions.

steps.title: Rebuild Without the Formula
steps.mastery: Recover a result from its reasoning when the formula is unavailable.
steps.practice: Derive the quadratic formula from completing the square on ax^2 + bx + c = 0, with the formula covered.
steps.detail: Work on paper with the source shut. Where you get stuck, note the line you stopped at, look up only that line, and carry on. The value is the record of where it broke — a derivation you can produce from scratch is one you will still have in a year, and the stuck lines are all you need to study.
steps.proof: A written derivation ending at x = (-b plus or minus root(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a.
steps.pitfall: Checking the next line each time it gets hard, which produces a copy rather than a derivation.

problems.prompt: In completing the square on x^2 + 6x + 5, what is added and subtracted?
You stall at 1 line of a 7-line derivation. What do you look up?
problems.answer: Only that line, then continue from it.

problems.prompt: Why is a 7-line derivation you can rebuild worth more than a formula you have memorised?
problems.answer: It survives being forgotten: the result can be recovered from the reasoning.

steps.title: Test With a New Case
steps.mastery: Apply a result to a case the examples never showed you.
steps.practice: Use the mole ratio method on a reaction you have never seen: 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3, from 0.60 mol Fe.
steps.detail: Understanding is what survives a change of surface. Pick a case with different numbers, different names and the same structure, and do it without looking at the worked example. If you can only do the version you were shown, what you have is the example rather than the method.
steps.proof: You get 0.45 mol of O2, and can say which ratio you used and why.
steps.pitfall: Choosing a new case that is the worked example with the numbers changed, which tests nothing new.

problems.prompt: From 0.60 mol Fe in 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3, how much O2 is needed?
problems.answer: 0.45 mol, from the 4 : 3 ratio.

problems.prompt: How much Fe2O3 does 0.60 mol of Fe produce in that reaction?
problems.answer: 0.30 mol, from the 4 : 2 ratio.

problems.prompt: You can do the worked example but not the same problem with new substances. State what you have.
problems.answer: The example memorised, not the method understood.

steps.title: Find What Breaks It
steps.mastery: State the conditions under which a rule stops holding.
steps.practice: Name 2 cases where "multiplying makes a number bigger" fails, with a worked value for each.
steps.detail: A rule you understand comes with its edges. Look for the case where a factor is 0, negative, fractional, or where a denominator vanishes. Write the value that breaks it rather than describing the case, because the number is the part you can check.
steps.proof: 2 worked counterexamples, such as 6 x 0.5 = 3 and 6 x -2 = -12.
steps.pitfall: Naming a case without working it, which leaves you unsure whether it really breaks the rule.

problems.prompt: Give a value showing that multiplying by 0.5 does not make a number bigger.
problems.answer: 6 x 0.5 = 3, which is smaller than 6.

problems.prompt: Where does "the square root of a square is the original number" fail? Give a value.
problems.answer: At -4: root((-4)^2) is 4, not -4.

problems.prompt: Why write the failing value, such as 6 x 0.5, rather than describing the kind of case?
problems.answer: The value can be checked; a description can be wrong without showing it.

steps.title: Two Ways to the Answer
steps.mastery: Reach one result by 2 independent routes and compare them.
steps.practice: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 4 twice: by formula and by splitting it.
steps.detail: Two routes that agree are a check on the arithmetic and on the understanding at once, because a wrong idea rarely survives being approached from a second direction. Where they disagree, the disagreement localises the error faster than rechecking either route alone.
steps.proof: Both routes give 32, and you can say which parts of the split correspond to the formula's terms.
steps.pitfall: Using the same method twice with different notation and calling it 2 routes.

problems.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 4. What is its area?
problems.answer: 32 square units.

problems.prompt: Split that trapezium into a 6-by-4 rectangle and a triangle. What are the 2 areas?
problems.answer: 24 and 8, totalling 32.

problems.prompt: Your 2 routes give 32 and 28. What does that tell you, and what next?
problems.answer: One route has an error; compare the corresponding terms to find which.

steps.title: Spot What Must Be Memorised
steps.mastery: Decide honestly which items no amount of reasoning will recover.
steps.practice: List 5 items from 1 subject that cannot be derived, such as the symbol Na for sodium.
steps.detail: Some things are arbitrary — names, symbols, dates, conventions — and reasoning about them is wasted effort. Getting this list short and correct means the memory techniques go where they earn, and everything not on the list is treated as reconstructible rather than learned by heart.
steps.proof: 5 genuinely arbitrary items, none of which anybody could derive.
steps.pitfall: Putting a derivable result on the list because memorising feels faster today.

problems.prompt: Is the symbol "Na" for sodium given or derivable?
problems.answer: Given — it comes from the Latin natrium and cannot be reasoned out.

problems.prompt: Is the boiling point of water at 100 degrees Celsius arbitrary or derived?
problems.answer: Arbitrary in that the scale was defined by it, so the number is a convention.

problems.prompt: Why keep the must-memorise list short, in under 20 words?
problems.answer: Memory work is expensive, and anything derivable can be rebuilt instead of stored.

steps.title: Explain a Wrong Answer
steps.mastery: Say exactly why a plausible wrong method gives the wrong result.
steps.practice: Explain why (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 is wrong, using a = 3 and b = 4 to show the gap.
steps.detail: Diagnosing an error is a harder test than getting it right, and it is the one that stops you repeating it. Work the wrong method and the right one on the same numbers, then name the missing piece — here the 2ab term — rather than only noting that the answers differ.
steps.proof: You show 49 against 25 and name 2ab = 24 as the missing term.
steps.pitfall: Stating the correct identity without showing where the wrong one loses its term.

problems.prompt: With a = 3 and b = 4, compare (a + b)^2 with a^2 + b^2.
problems.answer: 49 against 25 — a difference of 24, which is 2ab.

problems.prompt: Name the term that (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 drops.
problems.answer: 2ab.

problems.prompt: Why is explaining why a^2 + b^2 is wrong more useful than restating the right identity?
problems.answer: It names the step that fails, which is what stops the mistake recurring.
